author: henry
transcription:
Sept. 5th, 1861
Washington, D.C.

Dear Sister —

I received your letter this morning. Very glad to know that you are all well. As for myself, I have not been well, have not been able to drill for three days, but am some better now. The Dr. gave me medicine. I think it is very unhealthy sleeping on the ground. I have got so now I don't mind it much. This is a great place for fever and ague. I have got to be careful xx or I shall come down with it.

I can hardly realize that it is now fall. The summer has passed quickly away to me. It is nearly three months since I left home. It is now raining — shall probably have a wet day of it. We have a very fine tent to keepout the rain. I suppose you would like to know bout matters and things in our Camp. I shall write a Journal as soon as pay day comes around when I can get paper. When we get paid off again we shall probably have $24 or $26. I have now a five dollar gold piece. I shall send it all home except one or two dollars, by the Capt. as he expects to go to Champlain this month. Now I shall expect, of course, you and Mother will use what money you want. You must not hesitate, I put that down as a command. Times are hard and you will need it bad enough.

Our Regt. is stationed here as guards to keep the rebels from crossing the river. The pickets go out by Co. Ours has been out once. There are ten thousand of our troops three miles from here so that if we are attacked we can fall back and have a strong force. I have heard the opinion expressed that our Regt. may never see a battle, that we will always be stationed here as guards, but we can not tell. I for one am willing to go. I don't care where.

A sad accident happened here last Sabbath morning. A private from Co. H. was shot while on guard by another person. There were playing with their guns when one of them went off. He lived about fifteen minutes after he was shot. This makes three that have lost their lives by carelessness in this Regt.

I have received all the papers that have been sent from home. A short time ago I got two papers from Charles — New York Times. It is some time since I received any Observers. I don't doubt but what they all come, as the direction is correct. I have heard that we will have a band to our Regt. I hope it will be so, heretofore we had fife and drum. We have a very good drummer.

I hope you and Mother will take rides with our horse. He is very gentle if only managed right. I don't suppose he could run away if he should try. I hope the boys will get a chance to go to Middleburg. It is better than soldiering. Please write often.

Your aff Brother

Henry

Please let me know if my old clothes have been received. I sent them in a box with others that live in Champlain. I had mine directed to Mother.

transcription:
Sept. 27th/61

Dear Charles —

I received your letter last evening. I am getting along pretty well now. I have had the rheumatism very bad, am over it now. The reason I have not written about it before is I could not spell the word. It is a long word to spell. I hope you will always correct all bad spelling.

We have got a floor to our tent. It cost 95 cts. — that would make little over 30 cts for three of us. I should probably have the rheumatism now if we had not got the floor. I had it so bad before that, I could hardly walk, but I am all right now. It is raining quite hard today and it has rained all night. We do not have so much of it here as up North.

So Alexander is off for the war. Well, good luck to him. I rather think he will get sick of it when he comes to go on guard duty, but perhaps he wont. I was cut four hours in the rain on guard last night, but I have got so I don't mind it much. I came off from picket day before yesterday, was on with Lieutenant Scott and H. Cooper and Sergeant H. There were also two privates besides myself to stand guard, three hours and a half at a time. Had a very pleasant time while on picket. Our Regiment has not drilled for some time, but we will have three drills every day after this besides dress parade.

So you have heard about the attack over the river, but you did not hear it quite strait. There were not three Comp. of Rebels, but only thirty-five against twelve. I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand. We fare very well now, have bread every day, have a large oven to bake it in. We get our rations every five days. Each man gives two shillings a month for cooking. We have fresh meat quite often.

[page break]

Contd. Sept. 27, 1861

You wished to know how the men pass the time. Thus far they have played cards, but that is not allowed now. The Col. has forbidden it. There was to much gambling going on, so the boys can not play now.

I have nothing more to write now. Please send me a paper if it is convenient.

I remain your aff Brother

Henry

author: alexander
transcription:
Dec. 16, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Sister:

I wonder what sort of weather you are having up there. Pretty cold I guess, eh? The weather here is warm and sunshiney — very much like our September weather.

We came very near losing our Captain the other night but then "an inch of a miss", you know, "is as good as a mile." I feel very, very thankful that his life was spared to the Company. I hardly think his place could have been filled. The Major paid him quite a compliment the other day. He said to the Company "You have a good Capt." and that was a great deal for him.

Now I suppose you would like to hear how Capt. Ransom came so near losing his life. It was about as narrow an escape as I ever heard of. The only marvel is that he is now living. I can almost hear you say, "Out with it you provoking boy." Well, "here goes". The Capt. was going the "Grand Rounds". One of the officers is obliged to go over the line every night between the hours of one and six to see that the sentries are awake on their posts doing their duty and are properly instructed. This is called the "Grand Rounds". A freight train just then passed and as it was going slow he jumped on to ride out to one of the pickets about a quarter of a mile distant. (The freight engines on this road are different from those up North. They are fed with coal. The cabin is directly over the boiler which extends back so that the fireman standing upon a platform of the tender (which is open in front) is able to shovel coal into it. The Capt. stood upon the platform with the fireman. He (the fireman) had just commenced "firing up" when the boiler burst blowing the engineer, I presume, two or three hundred feet into the air. In his descent he fell through a tree breaking a limb about three inches in thickness, and on xxxx striking the ground he bounded and fell some fifteen or twenty feet from where he first struck. The Capt. stood still for a moment "thunder struck" I suppose when it occurred to him that the cars might come pileing one upon another, as they had been under some headway. He stepped off and started to go up the bank (about twenty feet in heighth.) When about half way up the body of a soldier (Haine, I believe) fell close beside him and pieces of the wreck all around him. If some of those large pieces had struck him they would have killed him instantly. The dome (weighing I should judge a ton perhaps, two, three or four) was thrown some thirty rods from the engine. The engineer was thrown about twenty-five rods. You can have some idea how high the men were thrown from the time it took them to fall.

The Capt. soon heard some one calling for help and immediately went in search of him. He found the fireman on fire and extinguished the fire by throwing water upon him from the ditch with his hands. The fireman died a day or two after. The Capt. is the only one that escaped alive of those upon the engine. He did not receive even a scratch. The fireman was so badly burned that he died, and Capt. Ransom standing beside him not even scratched. We certainly have great reason to be thankful.

Now, Miss Fannie, I want you to write me often — very often — once a week certainly. You tell James and Charles if they don't write me more often I will pull their ears for them when I get home. I certainly shall and they may look out for their noses, too. I have received four papers and letter dated Dec. 9 since I last wrote. You would never neglect writing me if you knew how much good that letter did me. Do not forget to send me some postage stamps to frank our letters. The ladies of Chazy are making up a box to send to those in the Company who came from there. I wish the ladies of Champlain would follow their example. Some warm woolen gloves would be very acceptable indeed.

Mr. Luther wrote Amos for a list of the names of those who came from Chaney. I do not have many idle moments. I am on guard duty tomorrow if all is well. I was up to Baltimore yesterday to church. I will tell you about it in another letter. I have sent my "picture" home. I will let you and Mother settle which shall have it. Capt. Ransom was very, very, very, very kind to me when I was sick. He came often to see me and brought me toast and tea a number of times. I wish Mother would write him a note. It would please him. Love to all.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander.

P.S. I see by the papers that there is danger of war with England. Let her come, I am as ready to fight Britons as Southerners. If she does interfere I hope my brothers and every other able bodied man will turn out and help us fight. I hope our regiment will be sent up the frontier.

author: henry
transcription:
Dec. 19th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Chas:

I received a letter from you and also two papers. We are having very fine weather for this time of the year. Our Co. came off from picket yesterday. The probability is now that our Regt. will stay here for winter quarters to guard the Potomac. That is what I heard. The Minnesota Regts. are fixing up for winter, building log houses. Our Regt. is also building a hospital. This looks somewhat like staying.

You wished to know who tents with me. They ar strangers to me. E. Graves from Chasy and John Green and A. Perkins. Pleasant fellows, but I would rather tent with some of the Champlain boys, but the tents are all full. I get very lonesome now and then. I go on line guard every week. We have three drills every day besides dress parade. We have also three Brigade drills every week. Three Regts. besides our march in line of battle, etc., etc. The old sutler was drumed out of Camp yesterday for selling licor, good for him, but some of the boys don't like it. We have one sutler in our Camp now. I have not got any tickets from him since pay day nor do I intend to. He charges to much. The boys cannot get anything to drink but cider now.

I am much oblige to you for sending me some of my money. I am not shure that I will get a pr. of boots. If I do not I think I will not use the money. In regard to sending money home — I paid 31 cts. freight. After this I shall send home my money in a letter. It is about as safe. I have not heard from Alexander yet. I have written him, but it seems that the direction is not correct. I shall write him soon. So far as I know the boys from Champlain like soldiering very well. Col. L--- has resigned so I have heard. Good many of the boys thought he was a coward. He has a very good voice. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx A good many of the boys pass away there time by playing cards, but I have not learned yet. If they are caught at it they are severely punished. Some of our Regt. were caught gambling the other night. They will have to stand on a barrel six hours without any food and four dollars taken off their wages. Write often. I am your aff. Brother,

Henry

author: alexander
transcription:
Jan. 28, 1862,
Baltimore

My Dear Brother:

You seem to be the next man in the "docket" to write to. I have "come to the conclusion" that I had better try. Mothers plan to write a little every day. In that way I shall have a letter done "before I know it".

I came off guard duty this morning. When I went on yesterday morning I was what some people would say, down sick with a cold. I feel much better this morning, and it is "my experience" that the best way is, to do your duty and whole duty, and you will feel a great deal better both in mind and body. At least I do.

I think our Regt. will leave here soon. I hope it will. Where we will go to, I do not know. All sorts of rumors are afloat. I presume you must have heard of the resignation of our Colonel (Hayward) long before this. Well may we be styled the "Orphan Regiment". But then I think we are quite as well off and a little better than when we had a Colonel. It is said that we have another Colonel (Green). I hope he will show himself a smart and brave man.

It is raining quite hard today. We have had no very very cold weather this winter, and very little snow. Just enough to make the roads muddy.

Feb. 4: I came off duty again this morning. I am now on every third day. We had quite a heavy fall of snow yesterday from the north-east. It made it very uncomfortable for me with my shoes, as every time I went out with the relief I filled them with snow and consequently went with wet feet. However, I feel quite well this morning. I like the snow and cold weather. It reminds me of home. I don't believe I could get along very well without frost and snow. The "South" is no home for me. Give me the North with its pleasant summers and fall and old winter.

I received two letters and a paper day before yesterday. One letter and paper from home and the other (letter) from Aunt Laurie and Cousin Nellie. You can imagine the pleasure they gave me. (I just received a letter from Willis Savage. I wrote him some time since. I now have five letters to answer.)

You ask me "what is the health of our Company". There was a time when there was quite a number on the sick list although it was not quite so bad as Mrs. Upton represents it. There has not been one case of the black measles in the Co. and I do not think in the Regt. though there has been quite a number of the red measles. The measles, I think, have had their run. Quite a number have died out of the Regt., but none from our Company. The reason I think is that we gave them better care. The hospital is no place to send sick men. They are not properly taken care of. One of our men (sick with the measles) was sent there. At one time he was so low that he was rolled over twice to ascertain whether he was dead or alive. You must not believe all Mrs. Upton or any other person tells you. My health is good. Luther gets along pretty well. He bought him a six shooter and sold it again with three dollars profit.

The boys say I am getting fat. Trudell is in the hospital. Lablue is getting along very well. We are doing hard service. I think I shall have a chance to smell powder before the war is over. I wish I was at home to enjoy the singing school, but then I am content here. How do you like Mr. Partridge?

I return you many thanks for your kindness in sending me the stamps. I feel anxious, very anxious, about James. I hope and think he will pass his examination. That examination will be very important in his life.

Our quarters are excellent. The entire Regt. is now in barracks. So it is decreed, is it, that the calf shall die. I am sorry that I am not there to raise it. I should indeed like to get a taste of the veal, but then we have plenty of fresh beef and I must console myself on that.

(Contd.)

Contd. Jan. 28, 1862

Drunkenness did prevail to a great extent, but it has been greatly checked since the Capt. has prevailed upon most of the Company to sign a pledge of total abstinence during their term of enlistment. You ask me how the men and I agree. Well, we agree pretty well, very well. The men generally obey orders very well. Trudell and I had a few words once. I was taking out the nine o'clock relief and having one man less than the required quota I was obliged to lengthen the beats. Trudell declared he would not walk the beat. I gave him and began to be quite noisy as Frenchmen usually do. I told him he would do as I thought best and that it would be good policy to have no more words about it. No, he would not walk it. No man could make him. Said I, "You can take your choice either to walk that beat or I will get a file of men and bring you to the guard house a prisoner." It was amusing to see how quick he "wopsid" around. He didn't care a --- how far he walked. --- I was the best corporal in the lot, etc. If I had reported him he would have been in a bad fix.

Give my love to Mother and James and Frances. Give my respects to Mr. Holcomb and the rest.

Your affectionate Brother

Alexander

be very pleasant for me if I should have to go, to be under your care, but I do not think you could stand it. You would be obliged to be on your feet most of the time, and I am afraid it would bring you down sick. There are others better able than you are.

June 13th, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Mother:

I received your letter day before yesterday. Very glad to hear from you and know that you are well. How I long to have one good meal at home, even if it wasn't anything but potatoes and salt, anything but hard crackers. I can not bear to look at them. As for fresh meat, I cannot eat it. I often think of what a good time I will have when I am at home. I have not been well for the last three days. Could not take anything but what I would throw up. The Dr. gives quinine and pills, but they have not helped me much. I am better this morning. Do not worry about me.

I suppose you have heard before this time of the Regt. going into battle. As I wrote the day after, the papers state we lost 150, but it was 123 wounded and killed. Our Co. lost two killed and ten wounded. I cannot be too thankful coming out without being injured. Lieut. Scott, I think, has gone home, as he was wounded. He acted very brave. Most of the boys were down on him before, but now they are all for him. Lieut. Ransom has command of the Co. now, as Capt. Reich has been discharged. I wish he was back. Ransom is liked very well.

This morning the rebel battery commenced firing bomb shells into our Camp and grapeshot. A twelve pounder was picked up this morning by one of our boys. The way the balls whiz around here is a caution. We have breastworks built in front of our Camp of logs and dirt thrown up against them. We have good protection from the shells. It is probably Gen. McClellan's intention to storm that battery before long, and then for Richmond.

I wonder how Sid can be so ugly about our cows. I am shure if I was at home seems to me if I was in Sids place I would put up with almost anything, but I suppose our cows are very unruly. They would never jump over Nyes fence, I am sure. I have not received a paper from home for some time, three or four weeks. Give my respects to Mrs. Brinkhoff. Tell her I hope to be home before winter. I do not feel able to write any more just now. I remain your aff. son,

Henry

June 13, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Charles:

I was very glad to hear from you and know that all is going on well at home. The weather here is very warm when it does not rain. I wish we had more of your pleasant weather and less rain, but we have to take it just as it comes. It very often happens that we have to be on picket when it rains.

You must have heard before this of the battle of Fair Oak. It was warm work there for a time. You can have no conception of how exciting it is to be in a battle. No one can except those that have been in. A perfect streak of reed placed all along the line. The firing reminds me very much of a number of men felling trees, only much faster. The ground shakes all around. All I thought of was to keep up in the ranks and load and fire. We very often had to load while advancing. I never knew till after we came out of the woods that any one was wounded or killed. There was a rebel Colonel and Gen. killed that night. Some say that there were three hundred of the rebles killed by our firing. There were two other Regiments engaged at the time besides ours. I did not go over the battle ground afterwards, but the ground was covered with the dead. I fired 40 rounds.

A secesh prisoner said that the road between here and Richmond was lined with carriages with ladies and gents. It was told them that Beauregard was going to capture six thousand Yankees and they came to look at them, but instead of looking at the Yankees they saw their own wounded pass and took the carriages to carry them in. They found it rather hot work. But I must stop, I do not feel well. I have the disentery very bad. I have not received a paper for some time. The secesh have thrown a good many shells over here this morning. One man was killed by a shell this morning at the hospital. I get perfectly disgusted with so much swearing in the Company, but I have to put up with it. I get lonesome now and then. Excuse all mistakes as I do not feel much like writing.

Yours truly,

Henry

June 16th, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Aunt:

It is sometime since I have written you but I hope to make up lost time. I have not been well for the last week. Been under the Dr.'s care, but I am better now and hope to be around again. Have not been in the hospital yet. The weather here is very warm most of the time.

It is a year ago yesterday since our Regt. swore in to the United States service. A long year it has been to me. Twelve more months and then our time is up. We may be discharged before that time, the sooner the better. There are not over five hundred men in the Regt. that do duty. It is needless for me to go into particulars about our Regt. going into a fight, as I wrote about it in Nellie's letter. We have had great praise from Gen. Gorman. One of the reble prisoners said he did not know how we could fire so fast, and load. They do not know the Yankees yet, but the are finding us out, to their sorrow.

Saturday, the day we had the fight, one of the rebles said their Gen. told his men to keep up courage as they were going to surmount the Yankees and take them prisoners. He said also that the road between here and Richmond was lined with carriages with ladies and Gents. to see the Yankees, but instead of seeing us, they had to take there own carriages to carry their wounded. It is my belief that they found it rather hot work.

We are having about as hard a time as we will have. Although we are not marching, hard crackers, salt junk, fresh meat I can not eat. The Sutler is sure to be around here pay day, but if there is battle, or any prospect of one, he is off.

We have breast works in front of our camp, but it is all the work of us soldiers as a matter of course.

So Uncle Henry is blessed with a boy. I am glad for his sake. I am sure for my part I would not object to a present of a few hundred, for the boys sake, and perhaps for his own good. He would not feel it much. Now I make motion we try it, but I do not want to have any responsibility. But enough of this for this time. My respects to all my friends. Excuse all mistakes with the hope of doing better next time. Believe me to remain your aff. Nephew.

Henry

June 22, 1862
Camp within Five miles of Richmond
Sabbath afternoon

Dear Mother:

I received your letter this morning, and very glad was I to hear from you. Nothing does me more good than to hear from home. I received the Obs. week ago today. It is very seldom that I receive a paper. I cannot see the reason as the direction is correct. I like the Observer better than any other paper. The New York Herald comes around every morning, but they are 10¢ a paper and I do not buy as I do not have the money and if I had I do not think I should buy them for they cost almost to much.

In my last letter I wrote about my health not being good, nor is it very good now, but I am better than I was. I have not been able to do duty for over a week. I go to the Dr. most every morning. He gives quinine and pills. I have had the disentery very bad. A great many in our Regt. are sick. Our Co. is on picket today, but I did not go as I do not feel able. We have hard bread and salt junk and fresh meat, coffee morning and night, soup for dinner, sometimes rice, beans and vegetable soup. I do not drink coffee, and as for hard bread, I do not eat much of that. It is very seldom that I eat meat. It is what I call pretty tough living. We have potatoes now and then. I can make them go first rate, but we do not have many of them. I shall make up for lost time when I get home. I believe I shall want to sit down and eat nothing but potatoes. The army is provided as well as it can be I suppose. I should like nothing better than to have my discharge, for your sake if nothing more. I have had about enough of it and long to be at home, but you must keep up courage. This war can not last much longer. When we arrive at Richmond they will have to give up. I take a great deal of comfort from the advice you give me in every letter. I know I have your prayers which comforts me very much. I was just thinking what a good dinner I should have if I was at home today, but there are better days coming I hope.

The rebles, from what I see in the New York Herald, are living on half rations and they are getting desperate. Most of them do not like Jeff or Beauregard and would desert if they could. There is a very large force in Richmond, not in Richmond but this side. We can hear their drums night and morning. Yesterday there was quite a skirmish between our pickets and the rebles. I have not heard the particulars yet. Our Regt. was all up in line. We very often are obliged to be up at midnight from their firing. Gen. McClellan is carrying a regular siege at Richmond now, starfing them out. I for one am about disgusted with soldiering, but I shall try to make the best of it. Take good care of your health. Do not go around to much. I am glad you dismissed the boy. He would be a great bother besides the expense. I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

I shall send extracts from my Journal next time and write to Frances.

June 30th, 1862
Camp near Sharpsburgh (?)

My Dear Mother:

We have just been mustered in again for pay. On looking over my accounts I feel a little blue. My expenses have been quite heavy. When we left Harpers Ferry we took only our overcoats and blankets in our knapsacks and did not receive the baggage we left until a few days since. How long I wore my shirt I am ashamed to tell you. Only I would say that I threw it away when I took it off. I purchased two shirts and two prs. of socks which cost me three dollars and a half. All my writing materials were completely spoilt by the wet and I have been obliged to supply myself anew from the sutler. A Corporal has often a need of a watch. One day while in Winchester I was sent with a guard of twelve men to the Academy Hospital to guard the sick rebels, some of whom were getting to be pretty strong. I borrowed a watch from one of our company with a cracked crystal. It fell to pieces during they and two hands were knocked off. I was obliged to have it repaired which in Winchester cost three dollars, of which I payed two, etc. etc. etc., all of which count up. When we are paid off I shall be able so far as I can now see to send you at least ten dollars to go to Charlotte with. I feel mad when I think how small it is. A truce to this subject as it is one not very pleasant for me to contemplate.

We are now encamped within about three miles of Strausburgh in a small fine woods. We have made ourselves little shanties of boughs which answer very well to keep of the sun and wind, but when it rains we fasten up a blanket which keeps off the greater portion of the wet.

July 1: July 1! I can hardly realize it. I thought last spring that I should be home by this time, certainly. Well, well, I am content to stay. There is the bugle for drill. The capture of Richmond has just been reported here. I hope it is true. I hope and pray that Henry has again come out unscathed. One of the boys heard the dispatch (to Genls. Siegel and Slow) read. It said that our forces had captured Richmond after three days fighting and that thirty thousand men were left on the field. I only wish our Regiment could have had a share in it. From present appearances I should judge that the whole army in this valley will move on soon. Our Capt. thinks we shall have some fighting soon now that Richmond has been probably captured. He thinks they will try and hold this valley. I shall be ashamed to meet Henry unless I have been in two or three battles.

I am enjoying excellent health. When we are paid off again I hope I shall be able to send home at least twenty dollars. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. Brinkerhoff. I feel very anxious to hear from James.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. Do not forget to remember me to Frances and tell her I hope to see her before long.

location: Camp near Harrison's Landing, James River

July 12, 1862
Camp near Haryson's Landing
James River

Dear Mother:

I received two letters from you the other day and was very glad to hear from you and that James had passed his examination. I sent ten dollars in two letters, five in each, but had no way of registering them. I hope you will receive them.

In my last letter to Frances I gave some account of our retreat. I will state some more of the particulars. When the sick were ordered to the hospital, McDonald came to me twice and urged me to go, but I did not feel like leaving the rest and so stayed. The battle commenced the last of June about five o'clock in the afternoon. We were counter-marching for some time before we came to the woods. We were then ordered on the double quick and had to throw our knapsacks. One of our officers, Billings, was sun-struck. I lost my cap in the charge. We came to a bayonet charge just as we entered the woods. Our regiment fired very low and did great execution.

The Irish Brigade charged a rebel battery — it was a splendid sight, shouting at the top of their voices. We lost a great many men, and the battery, ammunition, and provisions. We marched all the next day in a hard rain without a blanket. There are many who shirk the fights. The rebels claim a victory but I think McClellan managed very well. We were not whipped by any means.

Lieut. Webb has invited me to his tent. He is a very fine fellow. I should like very much to get my discharge but it is very difficult. I have now served thirteen months. If I serve my full time I shall receive one hundred dollars bounty and a land warrant.

My diarrhea is very bad. Sherman, who was head doctor, is now in Congress. Walker is head man now. We have a new doctor from New York. I received a letter from Alexander dated June 22nd. He was well, at Middletown. I hope Capt. Rich and Lieut. Scott will return for our company needs them badly.

David Savage wants a secesh bill. I have mailed James's letter to Alexander. Please write often.

Your aff. son,

Henry

author: alexander
transcription:
July 26th, 1862
Camp near Washington, Va.

My Dear Mother, Sister and Brother:

I received your letter yesterday and was glad to hear from you. I also received one from Frances a few days ago which I have not had time to answer. I was very glad to hear that she had returned home and was still in "good spirits."

Now as to Silas and Sid, I have a very poor opinion of such men. They are what I call fireside patriots. They are brave enough at home but let them come out here and you would see them whine. The idea of men at home finding fault while we are doing the fighting! There is a great deal of talk now about drafting. I hope they will draft every man that is able to carry a musket, and I believe they will.

Charles asks me if the military life is as miserable as it is represented. Well, I will give you my opinion. It depends entirely upon the disposition of the individual. If a man enlists and is determined to make the best of it, he will get along very well. But if he enlists and goes to grumbling about everything, he will be miserable. For my part I make the best of everything and am contented.

July 27th. Our First Lieutenant died last night at ten o'clock. It was a heavy blow to us all. He was a Christian Man and died like one. Sergeant Sterns said he "never saw so happy a death." Two of the regiment are being buried this morning. Luther is in the hospital, sick. I am in excellent health and am one of the hardiest men in the company. "Little Doolittle."

I was very glad to hear good news of Henry's conduct. Mother has no reason to blush at conduct of at least two of her sons. Love to all. I will try and give you an account of my adventures in my next. Remember me to Mrs. B.

Yours with affections,

Alex

P.S. I saw Luther this morning. He said he felt better. I hope he will recover soon. He is not dangerously ill.

author: mother
transcription:
September 21st, 1862
Champlain, N.Y.

My dear Henry —

Language is too weak, to express my anxiety about you since the commencement of the terrible battle. Than God your name has not yet appeared on the sad list, which has caused morning and lamentation to so many homes. I read the sad record day after day as it is published, with trembling. The record of yesterday shows that the 34th has been terribly cut up and that Co. B. has suffered severely, and yet you escaped, for which we cannot be too thankful to our kind heavenly Father. I trust you make Him your habitation. If you do the promise is "No evil shall come nigh you." "We shall only see it with your eyes." Trust in God until these calamities be over past. There is your only safety. Daily & hourly commit your all into His hands — He only can keep you & preserve you from all evil.

Poor Mrs. Carter is overwhelmed with grief at the death of her son. I hope you will write us immediately — and give us full particulars of all the battles that you have participated in — the most minute things that come under your observation, will interest us.

How I long to be near you. I am almost tempted at times to go down to the hospitals. If I was a man I am sure I should enlist. In reading the descriptions of the battle fields — my hair almost rises. I saw in the Herald of yesterday a sketch of the position of the two armies, in the battle of Antietam. As I looked at the location of Sumners Corps, I could but think of you dear revolting[s?]. How did you feel while facing & fighting that desperate army? Yet all impatience to hear from you — to know how you are after all you have passed through — as well as to learn from your own pen all about the battles.

I was perfectly delighted to learn through Alex letter — that you & he had met. That a meeting it must have been. Did you find him, or he find you? He only wrote a few lines, and gave no particulars.

I see the 60th Regt. has lost its Col. I see no report of any others being killed or wounded from that Regt. Perhaps it is to come yet. I hope you and Alex will see each other often as possible. Charles has not had his furlough yet, is to have a short one the last of this week. He has been made first corporal. I suppose they will leave for the seat of war next week. He seems to be quite contented so far — of course he knows nothing of hardships yet — and I think, never will experience what you have — and if he does not believe he will have an opportunity to win laurels on the field of battle as you have — for it is thought that the back-bone of the rebellion is broken. I think the war is nearly over. God bless McClellan — long live McClellan.

(Remainder of letter missing)

author: alexander
transcription:
Sept. 27, 1862
Hospital at Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother —

I suppose you will be both surprised and grieved to hear that I am in a hospital. I have had an exhausting diarrhea for several weeks past, which with the severest military duty has brought me pretty low. I feel much better today and think that with proper care and nourishment I shall get along finely. Orderly Dickinson was down here this morning and purchased some paper and some envelopes and a loaf of bread for me (with his own money). He is very, very, very kind to me. That bread will do me a world of good. I wish you could by some means or token express my gratitude to him. I can never forget his kindness and only hope I may find some means of repaying it. He showed himself every inch a man in the last fight.

I have heard from Henry. He is slightly wounded in the hand, but is still with the company. When I am able I will try and give you some of the particulars of the fight.

I am now, Dear Mother, going to ask a great favor, and it is only the stearnest necessity that makes me do it. Can you send me some money. You know, Mother, what it is to be away from home, sick among strangers and to be without money. I will not try to describe my feelings when I ask for this. You know them all. We shall have four months pay due us the first of Nov. ($52) and I shall be able to return it to you ten fold. Do you suppose you could spare me five dollars, if not, less will do. I will leave you to judge how painful it is for me to ask this of you. If you have not got it to spare do not send it. I do not wish you to deny yourself. I shall try and write often.

Your affectionate son

Alex F. Hubbell

Direct to Washington and I will always get the letter.

author: mother
transcription:
Sept — 28th, 1862
Champlain, N.Y.

My darling boys — (Alex)

I was shocked this morning by seeing Henry's name on the list of wounded, it did not state whether slightly or severely. I cannot tell you of the agony of mind I am in. , that I could fly to the darling boy, dear noble, brave, Henry. Want of means alone prevents my going starting for Washington. I do not know where he is — but I should find him. I do not know anyone in his regt. to whom I should write — Scott & Ashmond are at the hospitals. Of course I can get no information. My object in writing you now is to urge you to see him if possible immediately and administer to his wants. See that he is provided with every comfort. Write me

[page break]

immediately & relieve me from the agony of suspense. O, the dreadful minutes are hours to me — I do not know what to do with myself — and shall be miserable until I hear from you. I wish you would interest some one to get a furlough for him, if he is able to travel. O, if I could only go down and take care of him. Dear, say precious boy. Tell me what he needs. Get a furlough for yourself if possible — and come home with him. Tell me if I can come as a nurse. O, I wish I could, until he can come. My heart is aching to bursting, and I can write no more. I expect Charles tomorrow. It is heart breaking to think that I must so soon part with him. May God bless & preserve you, my precious boy, is the constant prayer of your aff.

Mother

..... 30 .....

Oct. 1, 1862
In camp on Bollever Heights

Misses Hubbell:

Madam yesterday there came a letter to the company fr. Henry and I seen the postmark on it Champalin. I took the letter in charge and I will Forward it to Henry when I learn to what hospital he went. I did not see him after he was wounded but made all the enquiries about him I could, as he and I had tented together for some short time before the day of the battle and slept together the night before. I find upon all the matters I can obtain in relation to him that he was wounded in the leg / a flesh wound/ and not very badly. He had been ailing for a few days before with his bowels and did not feel first rate. We all hope that he is properly cared

(Contd.)

Continuation of Oct. 1, 1862

for. Doctor Thurman went back from this place to see to the wounded and expect that he will return in a few days, and I will see him on his arrival and obtain all the facts from him and write you the true state of the case. I had thought that Henry would have written home immediately, so that you would have known where to direct your letters.

The 60th Regt. are on Loudon Heights about 2 or 3 miles from here. I seen ~~inRe~~ LaBlue of Capt. Ransoms Company a few days ago and sent his brother word of what had happened. I thought he would have come here to see me, but he had not come. No doubt but he would have liked to have come but perhaps he could not as it might conflict with his duty and also contrary to orders, as it is necessary at this point to keep the members of each Regt. as much together as possible, as we are only but a short distance, 7½ miles, from the Headquarters of Stonewall Jackson.

You may think it very strange and almost say neglectful that we know so little of your son Henry, but on due reflection when you come to take into account so many men congregated together as was on the very Memorable Day of the 17th ultimo and part in the woods, part in the clearance with the ever and constant explosion of shell, the noise of ~~xx~~ musketry, that of all sizes and the sharp crack and whizz of the Rifle ball falling as thick as hail, that it is utterly impossible to know about everyone that falls or is wounded. It is only after all is over when we call the roll of the Company that we can tell anything about them at all, unless perchance what comes under your own immediate observation. When a man gets wounded in action he falls to the rear and takes himself away to where he can take the best care of himself he can, and goes to the first ambulance Doctor or Hospital he can find. I therefore think that Henry went to Frederick, as a great many went directly there.

Having now said all that I can as a neighbor sympathizing with you all in your deep distress and hoping you will pardon me for such intrusion. I remain your obedient servant -

~~xxx~~ R. W. McDonald

author: luther
transcription:
Oct. 12th, 1862
Eckington Hospital
Washington, D.C.

Dear Alex:

It is so long since I have seen or even heard from you that I hardly know whether you are alive or not. How do you get along? Do you have good health? I have had a pretty long pull off sickness but am getting well now fast. I expect to be able to return to the company before long.

How are all the boys? There must have been some promotions lately, hasn't there? Do write and let me know who and what they are. It is so long since I have heard anything to speak of about matters in the Co. & Regt. that I would like to hear very much. Do you have much duty to do now where you are? I think I shall be able to stand it before long. I want to at any rate. Capt. Ransom was here to see me yesterday. Just from home and brought me some things that I was very much in need of. I was glad to see him looking so much better than he did the last time I saw him before.

Now Alex do write immediately and tell me all the news.

Hoping to see you soon, I remain as ever, your friend,

Amos C. Luther

author: mother
transcription:
Oct. 29th, 1862
Champlain, N.Y.

My darling precious pet:

Yours of the 20th I recd. this morning. I congratulate you on your promotion. It is very gratifying to me to see that you merit the rank of Sergeant, for I take it for granted that you could not have it, did you not deserve it. Dear, dear Henry was never dealt justly with. He was acknowledged by all to be a brave and upright soldier. Capt. Rich — I will not write what came near slipping my pen. He is now Capt. of the Co. to which Charles belongs in the 153 Regt.

I see B. Misner this morning and he has dashed any hopes with regard to Henry. He says that he and Albert are not incarcerated at all, and that they saw all the prisoners taken at Antietam, and Henry was not among them. Says if he was a

[page break]

prisoner he was left at some of their hospitals.

O, I fear that he was one of the "unknown" buried, or one of the number found in the bushes, who had died of their wounds and could not be identified. They did not cross beyond the lines of the 34th and he might in trying to escape to some place of safety have gone over. By hope that he is living is a forlorn one, but still I cannot give him up. I must hope against his end that he may be a prisoner. My darling, darling Henry. How I long to write him, & receive letters from him. If there is a possibility of getting information from any source as to his being a prisoner, do not fail to do it. You may hear through returned prisoners. Pray for him, daily, as though we know he is a prisoner — peradventure he may be. Pray that he may be returned to us soon and that God will raise him up & find a sympathizing friends in his bondage, heal his wounds & restore him to health. My prayer is, if he is living that God "will be a very present help to him at this his time of trouble." He must have him in the hands of the "Father of the fatherless," trusting that He will fulfill his promise to him, and be more than an earthly father could be.

The 153d Regt. left Fonda last Monday for North Carolina. I do not know when I shall hear from Charles. It saddens me sad, to have him so far away. My heart aches about Henry that I cannot endure, to have either of you any longer in the army. B. Misner talks very discouragingly about the war closing. Says there is not the least reliance to be placed upon the papers — the reporters are all liars! They write to produce sensation, not to keep up the spirits of the government, of the country rather. They told him in Richmond that they would fight to the bitter end! Surrender never!

If the papers are to be believed, there is another great battle impending. O, I hope you will not be in it. If you are — do not go in without your name upon your person. You are in peril — and I trust you realize the importance of being ready, of always having your "lamp trimmed." You must consecrate yourself anew daily to the Saviour. "Watch and pray." Commit yourself into the hands of God, as this living or dying you may be the Lords. Let his word be the man you counsel and guide of your life. Resist temptation, resist the devil and he will flee from you. Be sure he has a minister in the army, if all I hear is true, and he has a tremendous influence too. His examples are not scholarly and may almost vie with the General. O how rapidly he is peopling his regions from the army. Let all who love Christ then unfurl His banners — the rules of prayer. He hears then as well as privately. For mercy. Be a Christian soldier.

For my sake, take good care of your health. Had you not better get some competent person to measure your foot and send home for boots. Write what kind of ones — tell us just what you need — everything you need — and we will endeavor to send them. Do not suffer for anything.

Ben is Capt. Ransom not Luther. I have not heard from James since I wrote you last. He commenced studying yesterday and has not ceased yet. A o'clock this afternoon it is dismal enough. Charles has sent home his bounty money to be let. He can get no one to take it nor my interest. There are such fearful times ahead that people are keeping their stocks very snug. The Rail road is a success by and by.

Mrs. R. leaves next week and then we are alone. We still have little Joe stay here nights. If I could only hear from Henry, I could endure anything, every thing. Frances? friends in Longeurit[?] and Grand Ligne heard from Poussee[?] point that Henry was dangerously wounded. I am afraid he was wounded more seriously than was reported. There are several in the Regt. from Poussee "point." I can not learn that any one had spoke with him after he was wounded. You have not told me what your sensations were when you went into battle. God grant that you may never go into another.

[page break]

Kind regards to Capt. Ransom and Luther. Write me soon, very soon. God bless and preserve you from all evil.

Your aff.

Mother

Clark Copeland is sick of the typhoid fever. It is prevailing here quite extensively. I expect to hear from Charles in the coming week. I will then write you again and send his address. Tom called here the last week. He thinks Charles is not robust enough to endure the hardships of the soldiers. He was discharged for not being able bodied. They must be in North Carolina by this time.

author: alexander
transcription:
Nov. 12th, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother:

It is a long, long time since I last wrote you. I know you must feel very anxious about me, but I do not think you will blame me when you know all. A day or two after I wrote you my last letter we marched shifted our Camp and continued changing until at length we settled down on Bolivar Heights. I have been indisposed for some time and there my indisposition took a permanent form in the shape of Jaundice. I had very little disposition to write and did not wish to until I had something more favorable to write about concerning myself.

We left the Heights a day or two to guard Government property in this place where we now are. To "cap the Climax" I took cold and had my face break out in a way not to be envied. I suffered a great deal with my eyes and was sometimes afraid I should lose them, but they are better now though still very weak. I will write you a good long letter as soon as my eyes are stronger. I received your welcome letter of the 4th inst. last night. Will try and write soon. Capt. Ransom is very, very kind. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,
Alex. F. Hubbell

author: charles
transcription:
Nov. 18th, 1862
Camp near Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter directed to Fonda some days since & have received three since, the last dated Nov. 10th I received on the 15th. We will receive our letters without being delayed, I think, after this. I have recd. two Observers, also for which I am much obliged. The daily newspapers are sold here from 3 to 5 cts. each.

I am much pained that we hear nothing about Henry, but hope that he is a prisoner. I don't think he can be according to the surgeon's account. But we must make the best of whatever comes.

I wrote Jones yesterday & sent Alek's letter to him. Hope he will succeed at West Point, but if he does not it will be nice to have him at home. I do not think

[page break]

I will be at home very soon as the war does not look to me as if it would close this winter. Number of the men expect to go home next spring as they think the war will close by that time. Also a great many wish they had never enlisted. Yet Charles for one. A. Douglas & I are not sorry that we came to the war. But I think we will not go to the front this winter as our regiment is not well drilled & there is plenty of guard duty to be done. Unless a lot of new troops come to take our place we will remain here. There is a resort that we are to go into the city into the barracks now building to stay this winter. I don't know whether it is true.

Two regiments are now guarding the city. All citizens are allowed to come into the city, but none to go out except they have a pass. All soldiers are allowed to go in & out at it is a favorite their camp, but none to come into the city without a pass, after nine p.m. until morning none can pass either way without the countersign. I was glad that the Captains & Lieutenants have to be on guard duty also. I like to see them work. Their business is to pass the men on their post & to look after them once in a while to see that they are doing their duty. We are on 12 hours at a time outside the city. There are 2 or 3 men at a post so that the men can relieve each other. At night we carry our blankets, but it is cold to sleep on the ground & in the open air. No picket fires are allowed, but we find a fire sometimes where we can get warm. We come on duty nearly every day sometimes in the night & other times in the day.

Our Regt. guards the convalescent camp, also the parole camp & furnish a funeral escort for the soldiers that die in the hospitals. So that we have no drill now as there are not men enough. No liquor is allowed to be sold in Alex., but it is done privately — good many bottles of liquor are daily taken from the soldiers in the city & sent to the provost marshals.

A large number of our men are sick, some with one thing & some with another. The hospital here is in a tent. It is full & some are taken to the city. One sickly man enlisted & died not long after coming here. He bled at the lungs. His Co. sent his body home. He was from Fonda. It cost $50, for embalming & $25 for freight, making $45[sic]. His Co. raised $72, nearly every man paying $1.

Two corporals in our Co. have been reduced to the ranks, that is, had their stripes taken off for absences from camp without leave. Another had his stripes cut off for threatening to shoot his Lieut & then he was tied to a telegraph pole till he could behave himself. He was an ugly fellow. Our Co. Corporals are all right for.

I tent with James Lucas, Sam Pelky & a lot of Frenchmen. They all speak good English & are decent men. I was with A. Pouglias[?] some time when we had a change of men to fill up another tent. I heard that I was to go into this tent which was occupied by the worst men in the Co. But Lieut. Col. Frentress[?] made the change instead of someone else & I was put here into the best tent in the street. L. C. Frentress made quite friendly towards me. The men from Fonda do not like him. He is to strict I suppose. Col. Sabastine[?] has not been here since he came from. He has been sick, but is better. The officers boots are a short distance from ours, all in a row. Some of the men cook for them. Each tent has a corporal or sergeant in it. The tent I was in had three corporals so that it was unnecessary for some of us to move. There are a sergeant also with us. As there was no non officer in the at tent a sergeant was put in it & I got into a good place.

Mrs. Ruth Hubbell & sons prosper pecuniarily & otherwise. I think we had better not buy any of their land — so we have more land now that we can manage. And besides we have not more timber enough in all on [?] land I do not think it would be good policy to strip our land of growing timber. You speak of perishable property. I do not think that timber is that kind of property. Those cedars that have been cut ought to be drawn from the first snow. There is where we missed it last winter.

[page break]

Battiste will draw them perhaps, if not he may know someone who will.

That Plummer is a cheat. He owed us three loads at the end of last winter. They were small loads. I should threaten to sue him for trespass if he goes there again.

The weather is now drily, but it has not rained much yet. Over a week since, on Nov. 7 it snowed all day, but it was all gone the next night. I heard that it was more snow that they have had for some years. I think I shall buy me a pair of boots for the mud.

I think you had better dine out Thanksgiving if you are invited. You have lonesome times enough & ought to see company when you can. Frances must be full of business teaching French, etc. Fancy she likes Mr. Simons better than she did Mr. Karns. Has she got into a fight with that French teacher? I hope she will write & tell me all about her class & other things. Reed. her letter, will answer it soon. How is your health? Mine is good & has been good. My cold is better but is in a good place here to catch a new one. I hope that you will try to make yourself as comfortable as possible in every way. Two months & a half pay is now due us, but I do not know when we will be paid. Write soon & all the news.

Aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

..... 30 .....

author: charles
transcription:
Dec. 8, 1862
Camp near
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

As I am off guard today I will write to you. Guard duty at the city these cold nights is no fun. We are not allowed any guard fires now. The reason is, I suppose, that the soldiers steal all the wood they can get hold of. Have been burning the grave yard fence. There are three fires, one at each end of the pickets & one in the middle, but we are going to have guard tents put up with stoves in them so that the guard can warm themselves, I hear. There are 2 or 3 men put on in a place so that they can relieve each other. When we go on guard nights we put on our over coats & our blankets. I dont know as I can say put on our overcoats for we have them on nearly all the time. When three men are on a post two can put their blankets together & lay down, but I dont think any one will try it this cold weather.

There is snow on the ground a slight covering & plenty of ice. A creek near us thot running into the Potomac is frozen over solid that we might have good skating if we had any skates. But it will not last long, I think. Food is scarce here. We got out of wood so we went to a fine piece of ashwoods, young trees about as large as my leg, & carried it to camp. It was a pretty large piece of woods, but they came from the convalescent camp in a steady stream all day to hack it & to their camp which is some ways off. Our men & theirs have cut this woods all down. There are 10 or 12 thousand men in the convalescent camp sick, convalescent, & well. The camp is about to be broken up, the well men to return to their regiments, some to return to the hospitals & some to be discharged. This camp we call loose hill.

Capt. Rich is now Aid De Camp to Gen Slough who is military governor of Alexandria. I suppose Rich's employment is till we leave here, but I think from the looks of things we will stay here this winter. The officers are fixing up their tents to well to leave soon.

You wished to know if I was detailed as funeral escort. I was detailed one day, but did not act as there was no death. 26 men were detailed daily as funeral escorts, but there are more detailed now. They went to the provost marshals office where they were told if there were any deaths. The escorts that was to butt of the provost M. office all day if they had nothing else to do, for a funeral might take place any time.

I am glad you have found that memorandum book. When us boys get our pay you will have some figures to put down. I signed an allotment roll at Fonda allotting $10 a month to you. Have it the men signed it. I wrote Jake a few days ago. Received your letter of Dec. 1st, also the Observer. The Observer is like an old friend. I have just seen Ben Bouron & Freeman Houron. Ben is going to Yorktown

[page break]

if he can get a pass, to see his brother Lyman. Ben says it cost him $16 to come here. Will you send me a little woolen yarn & a couple of darning needles if you send me anything. Mrs. Doolittle says he does not have enough to eat. Says he eats when he can cook for himself. Says the men are lazy. Says that each man cooks for himself.

We went down to the city & went through it, but not a thing could we buy as neither of us had a cent of money. There is nearly 6 months pay due Alek & nearly 4 months due me. I dont know when we will be paid. Uncle has poor I guess. The men in our reg. are being trusted by the sutler. I shall not trade with him as he sells to dear. He has good butter, but it is 40 cts. a pound. Some of the men in our tent buy it. Alek says he owes the sutler $11.00 — had to buy as they could not get enough to eat.

We have just received our rubber blankets. I am very glad for they are just what we need. I have been very lucky about getting wet — have not been wet yet. I mean the time very well when not on duty. Riley from Corbeaus has papers sent to him which I read. With a good fire in the stove & a canoe to read I make out first rate. When we are on guard at night we are excused from any duty the next forenoon when we stretch out on the floor, feet to the stove, & try to take a nap, but we are pretty sure to get woke up by the mates. They say that one of the Fonda companies, the Captain I mean, cheated the Government by taking some men of another Co. & putting them with his to fill out his Co. till they had been inspected & drawing the bounty for three men who did not belong in his Co.

I have not been home sick since I have been here. Am glad that I am not a family man as they are the ones who are homesick. I bet Staats says if he ever gets home they will not catch him again — he will not be such a fool as to enlist. The soldiers here all seem to hate the niger. They say it makes them mad to think they are fighting to free the niger. We have a small brass band & a lot of drummers so that we have music mough. Hear it every day at dress parade & guard mounting. I guess you forgot that Alexandria is a large city. I can see and can buy almost anything here. I should not feel anxious about James if he does not succeed at West Point. He will in something else. I wish you would write all about home matters.

[page break — Dec 13 continuation]

Dec. 13, 1862
Camp near Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter last evening. They always come in the evening. Are brought to each man by some one of the Co.

I was very sorry to learn that McDonalds story about Henry was not true. I was afraid when you first wrote of his story that there was some mistake. I still think he may be in or prisoner in some rebel hospital. Probably he was badly wounded. Savagham heard from Mathews that his brother was most likely in a hospital. Bethune belongs to Capt. Rich's old Co. He was not in the battle as he was in the hospital at the time. I saw him in Washington when our reg. was coming here. Also saw him not long since here. He had cut from a newspaper a list of the killed & wounded in his Co. at the battle instances[?]. He showed me the list of killed & wounded. Came here to see Capt. Rich. A stayed here with him a day or two. I did not see him long either time. Both meetings were accidental & he introduced himself. Savagham heard from Mathews, not since if we had heard from Henry. McDonald's report might have started at Champlain. Somebody might have wrote to their friends in the army about him. Mr. Cook might have written Albert & he some one else in Co. B.

[page break]

About horse beef; we do not have any. We have salt beef which I like when the salt is all out. That is, when it is well cooked. Some call it salt horse.

We are not going to North Carolina. I don't think anyone believed we were. The regiment will stay here all winter. We have just had guard tents put up around the city for the guard. There is a fire in each tent & the guard relieve each other. We have also our rubber blankets so that we will be quite comfortable. The guard stays at the city 24 hours. We have boiled fresh beef about four times a week. Each man has a loaf of bread a day which he puts in his haversack. The bread sells in the city for 5 cts. We have boiled rice quite often which I like. It is sweetened a little. A good many of the men dont like it. We have two good cooks now.

I think we will not get our pay till next month. Wish you could send me one dollar. I have sold two dollars for repairing my watch. If that box comes will you send me two pairs of wool socks & two cheap handkerchiefs. They will be plenty. I have 3 prs. of socks but they will wear out before spring. A good many of the men have drawn socks. Some of them were thick & good — others not so. If not convenient dont send them as I can get socks etc. here.

I have not heard from sick yet. I do not like to write letters so Uncle John need not write often. I mean letters to strangers. Has Pollard married Mary Ann Brinkerhoff — you know who I mean. "I. Staats heard so from home. Have you engaged any one to draw those down saw logs. They ought to be drawn the first snow. Neshan will draw them or know of some one.

About James: I hope he will succeed, but if he does not it need be no disgrace. All are not calculated for military men & besides a good many smart men have not succeeded there.

I have seen some paroled prisoners (there is a camp of them not far off), but it would be useless to ask them about Henry as if they saw him they would not notice him as he was not in their Co. We have a good Chaplain. He has only preached to us two short sermons so far. & his sermons ought to be short as the men are drawn up in hollow square & stand. I mean 3 sides of a squad. The Chaplain stands in the 4 side & the officers also. He prays without kneeling. Some of the soldiers sing out of the soldiers hymn book. The Chaplain is quite sick now, caught cold at a soldiers funeral. The Catholics in our Co. attend church every Sunday in the city under the charge of the 1st Lieut. who is a Catholic. I dont know as there is a service anywhere else in the city.

I hope you will write often. You & Frances must make yourselves as comfortable as possible. We do not suffer from the cold as we have good fires. Our tent is a good tight one.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Dec. 21st, 1862
Camp near
Fairfax Station

My Dear Dear Mother & Sister:

I must "hurry up" and write or my fingers will soon be so numb that it will be wholly impossible. How I long to see you and when that will be God only knows. I wrote you a few lines the day before we left the Ferry. Since then we have done no small amount of marching. We went up Loudon Valley to Hillsborough, from there to Leesburg, thim to Fairfax Courthouse, from there to Dumfries, five miles from Aquila Creek and twenty-four from Fredericksburg. The orders were countermanded, I am one, and we marched back to this place, leaving a detachment of the Regts. there and another small force at Bolts ford over Bull Run Creek. We reached here day before yesterday and will probably leave soon.

Please thank Mrs. Hoyle surely for me for her kindness in sending those papers. Tell her that they were the sources of the greatest enjoyment to myself and comrades. The Plattsburgh paper was especially welcome. Say for me that we had the abolitionists quite as badly as does the editor of that sheet, and that we would much prefer fighting them to the Southerners.

You ask me, Mother, about my new duties: I could hardly tell you on paper, that you would understand, only that my responsibilities are much greater. Mother, did you ever receive the letter of two sheets I sent from London Heights telling you of my visit to the Camp of the 34th and all I learned there concerning Henry? I presume you did. I do not remember who they were that said they saw Henry. The boys (a number of them) said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and threw him self down. I think there is a strong probability of his being yet in a rebel hospital.

The first of January there is six months pay due me and I do not see much prospect of my getting it very soon as the treasury department does not seem to be in very good order. I am sorry for I should like to send you some money to get winter necessities. Mother, if you can without inconveniencing and denying yourself send me a little — and only a little — money, it would be a great comfort to me, and when you write if you will see and then put it in a stamp it will enable me to answer your letters much more readily for it is very difficult to get them here.

Love to all. I will try and write again soon. I am enjoying excellent health.

Your affectionate son,

Alex. F. Hubbell

author: charles
transcription:
Dec. 26, 1862
Camp near Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I was surprised yesterday to receive a visit from Alek. Day before yesterday Capt. J. B. Ransom visited our Co. He told me then Alek stood in his first place. I asked him if he could let Alek come & see me. He said he couldn't if they did not leave, but said I must come up & see him. I told him I would if I could. His reg. is at Fairfax station, 15 miles from here. The whole army corps is there. I did not think of the railroad as a means of going there & thought of but two ways of my going there on foot — or hire a horse. But I had no money to hire a horse & would have to get a furlough of two days to walk there, so I was afraid I would not see Alek, but he came here on the cars free of expense. He arrived here at 4 p.m. yesterday & left at 11 a.m. today. He looks well, though the eruption he had on his face has not entirely cleared out & also a little whiskers. He is also rather fat. I intend to get a pass & take a railroad ride to see Alek if I can. I gave him half of the butter & currants, some of the g. snaps, a little

[page break]

yarn & a d. needle with the two fingered mittens & a towel as he had nothing to wipe his face with, also a testament. While at Fonda I bought a matt of kid gloves so I have both mittens & gloves. Alek says he does not have enough to eat always. Says he each man cooks for himself. Says he lives on fat pork & hard crackers, though if they have a tin like they fry it on the plate. Also says that he is in a log barracks coffee drinker though they do not get much sugar to put in it. They now have dried apples. He says they live in the open sir as their tents are only large enough to sleep in. Two sleep in a tent.

We went down to the city & went through it, but not a thing could we buy as neither of us had a cent of money. There is nearly 6 months pay due Alek & nearly 4 months due me. I dont know when we will be paid. Uncle has poor I guess. The men in our reg. are being trusted by the sutler. I shall not trade with him as he sells to dear. He has good butter, but it is 40 cts. a pound. Some of the men in our tent buy it. Alek says he owes the sutler $11.00 — had to buy as they could not get enough to eat.

He received the box Dec. 22nd. Alek & I are much obliged. The currants & butter will go well & the snaps have & will go well for a short time. Quite a number of boxes have been received in our Co. & a great many in the reg. One box in our Co. staid 3 or 4 weeks in Washington & some of the eatables are spoiled. Did you pay my charges on the box ? if so how much. Snakes stuff filled up about half of the box. I have sent quite a number of acquaintances since I have been here. Albert Cook has been here. He M.& N.M. there are at the parole camp at Georgetown. Albert looks well, was going to try to get a 20 days furlough to go home. He rode a horse which was one of forty he & Bright took care of, as he told it. I was on guard & did not see much of him. J. Douglas & Albert went into the city. Cyrus Kellogg has been out of the hospital only a short time & is not at the convalescent camp. He has been here several times to see his uncle Norman. The convalescent camp has been moved to about 3 miles from here. There is a shanty there dug out the side of a hill. We had a good fire obtained by asking for a few sticks from each wagon that passed. I hope you and Mother went to Grandmothers as I think you would have had a good time.

Col McMartin said to us the other day that he thought we had no more months here among 800 men that[?] there could be at home among the same number of men. Said we a great deal better off here than we would be at the front in smaller tents. Thought we would stay here this winter. Alek said it made him feel bad to see how comfortable we were & then think of their own camp. Lieut. Burdick came with Capt. Ransom into our Co. I see Burdick quite often. He is a pleasant man. Frances old friend S. Tombe is going to be discharged. He was to be drummer, but has not drummed any. I suppose she remembers what a handsome man he was. Well, he looks the same as ever. Made some particular enquiries about Frances said she went to school when he did & did him a favor when boys were reciting to Mr. Dixon in the teacher class. Tombe became confused & could not answer his question when Frances went on with the lesson as if he had answered right. He told me he was invited to Mrs. Nodiah Moores to a party when C. Walkerton boarded there. Mrs. Vanberton[?] urged him to come & see Charles as he was very polite. He & his brother are both married.

Where does Mrs. Brinkerhoff stay this winter. Has she said you the rent? Mount Vernon is about 8 miles from here. Some of the men have been there. I dont know as I care enough about it to walk there. We had no drill Christmas, nothing but dress parade which we have every day unless it rains. Some of the men went to the Catholic & some to the Episcopal churches on that day. Our 1st Lieut. McGuire is a Catholic & takes a squad of men every Sunday to the Catholic church.

[page break]

At dress parade we have to have shoes blacked, clothes brushed & look as nice as we can. I staid in camp Christmas & at 4 p.m. Alek came. We have 3 men standing on a barrel (each on a barrel) to punish them for having to much of a Christmas. The slave men in Alexandria is a terror to our men. The worst ones are showered. One of our men was on city guard & put down his gun for a few minutes to get a drink when an officer came along & took it his gun. He was shut up in the slave pen & showered.

Washington is about 8 miles from here. It is difficult to get a pass to go there. I think we can get none unless it is on business. How do you & Frances get along? You know I suppose your ears are not jarred by the noise in the stone castle unless it is by the mice. You had better keep money going. It still do you good to take sleigh rides. How does Frances like going to the post office? I wish she would write & tell how the examination went off & all the rest of the news. I hope you still feel well.

Savagham did not write that letter that you read. It was written by Tromby. There are 12 men in our tent & only three can write. Sergeant Welky, Jim Lucas & myself. Those men that cannot write send more letters then I do & receive letters very often. I have written some letters for them. They think as I do that I am not a very rapid letter writer. Some of them all give you a letter to read & tell you to answer it. They dont tell you anything to write so you write what you have a mind to. The majority of the ignorant men are in our tent. I think that the other tents have not so many ignorant men in each tent as there is in ours.

Please write soon & all the news.

Your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell.

..... 30 .....

author: charles
transcription:
March 19, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

Your letter of March 10th received; glad to hear from you. I have not heard from Alex since I saw him. He is not a good correspondent and I am not one either as I promised to write him and have not done so. Last night I had just come from changing the one o'clock guard when a man fried fire. One sentry ran across the road and pounded on the door of the engine house with his gun crying "Fire." This engine house and the two steam fire engines it contains belong to Uncle Sam. This engine house and the steam fire engines are new engines, just

[page break]

come. Well, as the horses are kept harnessed night and day and fuel in the engines ready for the match, the engines were soon at the fire with steam up ready to commence throwing water. The engine hose was screwed on to the hydrant and a stream of water began to play on the burning houses. I heard that a Captain's wife living in one of the houses had several hundred dollars in money burnt up. The engines prevented the spread of the fire so that only four buildings were burned, thanks to Uncle Sam's engines, which were brought here to protect govt. property. There are only two posts where we have sentries, one at the door where we go into our camp and the other in the city guarding some guns. Two corporals a day are on, each taking half the day and half the night. We are having easy times and I hope we will stay here.

No liquor is allowed to be brought into the city except for hospitals and the private stores of officers. But it is sold slyly still. Some of our men got drunk; they were taken to the provost marshall's office and compelled to maser where they got their liquor. The result was that an Irish woman who sold the whiskey and one of our men were sent to the slave pen for ten days. There is a corporal here by the name of Beardsley who, our orderly says, is a great fool, only he don't know it. Tells about when he taught school so that he was called school master by the serpeant at Plattsburgh. He is a conceited but a good natured fellow. Well, I have received three wrappers from his sister. I did not know that he had a sister till I had received a paper and asked him. I think she may keep sending if she wants to, but I will not send her an entire stranger, any letters. She is careful to put her name on the papers.

I received two Tribunes today; have received two before, so that I have not read all you have sent. I find the Tribune interesting. I also read the Observer a few days since. I saw in the Tribune that mothers can receive a pension for a son that is killed provided that they are dependent or partly dependent on him for support. Savagham has never been heard from.

When do you think the war will end? I hope that we will give the rebels a good thrashing before long. The news is good from Vicksburg if it is true.

My health is very good at present. Alex Douglas complains of a headache for a day or two. Will you send me two dollars immediately if you have not done so, as I borrowed $2.00 about three weeks ago to be paid in about a week which I was not able to do. I hope Frances will write soon. How is her health and yours good? We now ride to the convalescent camp in the cars and bring the stragglers, as we call them, back, in the cars. We go up in the freight cars, no seating and come back with them naked inside and out, — that is, on top of the cars. The stragglers call us $800.00 and a cow, because the soldiers guarding that camp are now nine months men and receive $500.00 bounty. How did Silas' speech go off?

[page break — Mch 20 continuation]

Mch. 20 — I received a letter from Alex this morning enclosing one from you with $3.00. I send you the envelope to show you how it was directed. I suppose the Postmaster at Champlain put on the figures 113th and 60th at the top. Alex was well. You speak of my having wet feet. I have not had wet feet more than once or twice since I enlisted. I wear shoes because they are easier for the feet, I think. Think I shall sell my boots. Twelve of our men have left today for Fortress Monroe as a guard on the boat; took 4 days rations with them.

I don't think the land Mr. Rye claims has any maple trees on it. La Vally I don't think would be a good man. I saw in the Observer that the names of 400 Union soldiers who had died in rebel hospitals was about to be published. I think it would be well to see the list.

..... 30 .....

author: charles
transcription:
April 11, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your and Frances' letter of Mch. 29th in due time. Glad to hear that you both are well. My health is very good.

Yesterday all the soldiers were mustered that are in the U.S. service. The regiments are to be filled up by a draft. I think Uncle Sam will draft so as to have men enough to soon end this war. I see that we are about attacking Charleston, but I think it will be long before we take it. It is a strong place. Our reg't. has just received new guns. They are long Enfield rifles. These guns have the iron maw all well blacked which prevents their rusting. Our old guns we scoured the black off which made them look better as the barrels were bright, but a great deal more work to keep them clean. I hope that we will not be ordered to brighten our new guns.

The man from our Co. that went home to Plattsburgh on a furlough from our Co. has not come back; goes to Canada, we all think. Another Plattsburgh man has now got a furlough from our Co.

We commenced yesterday to fire at a target. Our reg't. at battalion drill fires blank cartridges. It is afraid our Co. will get behind the reg't. in drilling, but we will have Co. drill soon, I think. Ten men and two sergeants go every afternoon to the convalescent camp for stragglers.
