They bring them to the soldier's rest where they stay till morning, then take the mail steamer to the creek. Then ten fresh men and a sergeant go with them to the creek. Our men bring two or three hundred stragglers a day from the distributing camp which is close to the convalescent camp. We corporals have an easy time as we don't have to go to the creek or to the distributing camp. We are on duty about three days, but the duty is light. A few days ago I received three Tribunes and the Observer.

I have just seen Freeman Bowron. He came from Washington where his Co. is to see us Champlain boys. Looks very well and says when his three years are out he will reenlist in the regular army. He is orderly sergeant in the cavalry. Says his captain dated his commission as orderly back two months before he got it. If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in. I am afraid he was killed.

I have not heard from Alex for some time. Think Hooker's army will soon march. The weather today is too warm for comfort, but the nights are cold. Need all our blankets at night.

I hear that hay is $20.00 a ton. Your arrangement about the horse and cow was a very good one. Have you had any sugar yet? Seems to me there are not many maples on the strip of land Mr. Rye claims. If the land is not his, he ought not to have it. Mr. Crea claims a corner; he is a hard man, very close.

What does Mr. Copeland think of ministers being drafted? I don't agree with Alex about Silas and Sid. Think they would be very foolish to enlist. I have not got sick of soldiering yet; will not, I think, till the hard times come. Hope our Co. will stay here this summer. Please write all the news. Did you see Charles Dodds? He says he would not stay home for anything. It is too lonesome.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: charles
transcription:
April 27, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcomed letter of April 17th a few days since. Also one the same day from Mary McNeil. I found the Tribune interesting. I'm sorry that you think I did not receive your letters. I assure you your letters are very welcome. Today is Sunday and we are blockaded by the snow storm. There is about six inches of snow on the ground and it is snowing hard and blowing. I am glad that our men have not to go off today. This snow will all go off at once and make lots of mud which we will have to wade through to go to the distributing camp for the stragglers. A few days since we had a hard snow storm. The snow quickly went off and left us some awful roads to travel. I found then that shoes were not the thing. I wish you would send me two dollars as I want to buy a pair of boots.

You ask me what makes me think Henry was killed. Well, I think so from what you have written me. Think Scott, the tailor, is strong evidence. Right before last I was at the soldier's rest; got a talking with one of the stragglers and he told me he belonged to Co. D, 34 Regt. I asked him about Henry and he did not seem to remember the name, when a soldier close by said he was killed, that he saw the name on a headboard at his grave. This soldier's name is Abram Fry, and he belongs to the last N.Y. artillery. I asked him the stragglers's name. He said the artillery waited after a battle because their sessions carried the shovels, picks, etc. The man belonging to the 34th was hurt at the battle of Antietam, has been in the hospital at Philadelphia ever since. There are only two besides him that are sick, though not with the small pox. I hope you will write me soon again.

I only heard last night that the 60th reg't. was about a mile from Aquia Landing, so I started this morning to see him, but with what success I have just told you. I hope Alex is uninjured. Have been searching to hear about him for two or three days. Two days ago I saw the 16 Reg't. N.Y.V. on board a steamer that stopped here for some old clothes they left here boxed up a year ago. The reg't. was on its way home. discharged as its time was cut out. The men looked hard; that is, they were tanned and clothes very dirty. They belonged to Sedgwick's Corps. Said it on coming out of the woods the first thing they knew the rebs fired a volley into them. This was from the first line of battle which then laid down and the second line fired and laid down in turn, and then the third line fired. Then they had three rebel volleys in a few minutes. They belonged to Sedgwick's Corps.

I saw George Corbin with the 126th Reg't. You say that you want me to go over the battle ground of Antietam. I don't know where this battle field is, and don't know who would go with me that knows where the 34th reg't. fought. As for his Fry, his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now. I think there is not the least doubt that Henry was killed. We would have heard from him long before this if he had been living.

Every day reg'ts. are going home, their time being out. I guess we will stay here all summer. Hope we will for we are having a good time. If the cavalry come on here and the satisfaction of sending us up is in a short time should be blighted. He was so happy in the prospects; said he should begin to count the days soon; dear, dear Henry, my darling boy. Oh, what a pall is over my heart, and must be while I am in this vale of tears. But my pilgrimage is nearly over. Already the loved ones who have gone, are bearing me home.

[page break]

I guess Dan Moore bothers you about this sugar business. Don't you judge Dan rather harshly? If you don't get enough sugar — why, it can't be helped, and let it go. I have finished Vermont's Pride and think it is a good story. Read the Tribune and Observer yesterday and 3 Observers not long previous to this. I think that I receive them all now. Doesn't Alex want some of these papers? Perhaps Mrs. Hoyle forgot to send him any papers. We are having fine warm weather now. The grass is green, flowers are in bloom, and lettuce is fit to eat.

Give my regards to Mrs. E. Hubbell and family when you see them. Enclosed is a $40 allotment check.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: mother
transcription:
April 30, 1863
Champlain, N.Y.

Dear Sir:

My son, Henry Hubbell, of Co. D, 34th N.Y. reg't., has been missing since the battle of Antietam. He fell as the enemy charged, and was not seen after. The surgeon assures me that he sent trusty men to search the field after the battle, that every union soldier killed was fully identified, and that my son certainly was not among those. His belief is that he was slightly wounded and taken prisoner.

The Col. thought he was taken to the hospital. He was in very feeble health some time previous to the battle.

The Rev. ---- advises me to write to you with a request from him to ascertain if possible, where he is, or may have been. If he is not living, it would be a great satisfaction to me to know when and where he died, whether in one of our own or a rebel hospital. I have noticed in a late paper that many of our soldiers are in an insane asylum at Williamsburg, Va. I sometimes fear he may be among them. He was of an extremely nervous temperament, and very much reduced in health.

That the Lord will direct and give you success in this matter, is the prayer of his afflicted/ mother,

Frances M. Hubbell.

author: alexander
transcription:
May 16, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Charley:

I received your letter of the 3rd just after we returned from the front and was pleased to hear of your safety. I feared you had been obliged to leave Alexandria as it was reported here that the army had received strong reinforcements from Wash. and Alexandria. I hope you may never be called away from there.

Our reg't. was pretty roughly handled at Chancellorsville, May 3rd. We lost seventy-three, nine killed, forty three wounded and twenty-one missing. Co. H lost six men. Lester Bond (Co. B) was shot through the forehead and instantly killed while the reg't. was making a bayonet charge. Our Orderly was sent Fittingly a few feet in the air, by a rebel shell, but without doing him much damage. The reg't. charged three times upon the rebels, driving them back each time in great disorder. The eleventh corps broke and ran in a most cowardly manner and let the brunt come upon the twelfth. At one time, the 60th and 102nd N.Y. were left unsupported by the rest of the troops and for a long time held the enemy in check.

I received a letter from home today. They are all well. When I sent my money home I asked Mother to send me a watch. She tried to get one, but Scott had none much as I sent. Mother says she received a letter from you saying that you could get one, but you see that will do no good. I have my money home and so have you. (I sent forty-three dollars and ninety cents). The watch I used very much as you well know, and I must have it. Will you, Charley, if you have but two stamps, write Mother to send the watch without delay. Now Charley, if you do this, you will do me the greatest favor imaginable. Send it as soon as you can, for I need it very, very, very much. Give my regards to all the boys from Champlain.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. We are camping in the same place as when you were here.

..... 30 .....

April 13th — I could not mail this letter for want of stamps. About that watch. I wish you would send it as soon as possible. You had better send it by express. The mesh of one gloves me sometimes in a very awkward position. When on guard duty I am obliged to guess at the time my reliefs have been on post. My portfolio with my papers, pens, postage stamps, etc., etc. (on acct of my being on duty) Luther carried in his knapsack were lost in the late battle, owing to the fact that Luther was obliged to throw away his knapsack.

It is reported that the rebels are in full retreat. Our corps suffered severely in the late battles. A large number of reg'ts. have gone and are about going home so that the 10th A.C. is considerably reduced in numbers. If there is truth in the report that Hooker has crossed the river (and I think there is) I think the reason that we are left behind is to keep open the avenue of supplies to the army — though we may be ordered on any moment.

I will endeavor to write soon. My regards to all friends.

Monday Morn. — May 14th —— The rebels commenced shelling the hospitals and the supply and ammunition trains, but did not keep it up long for our cavalry made a charge and captured the two rebel guns (breach loaders). I think I have great reason to thank God for my safe preservation. The same day the trains were moved farther back from the river.

Please let the Capt. know the loss of the company — L. Bond, killed; G. Ploof, wounded; H. Myers, wounded; P. Brookway, ditto; I. Stone, missing; B. Brame, Orderly Sergeant Brookway is still with the company. Luther was uninjured.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
August 16, 1863
Capitol Hill Barracks
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

It is a long time since I wrote you and the reason is we are all very busy. We are on guard from one to two days at a time. Still I might write while on guard if I could carry the writing materials with me. I have received no letter from you for a long time also, but I suppose I can't say anything as I have not written you.

Our Reg't. guards two prisons and has a guard at the R.R. Depot, also has a camp guard, and besides a large number of men go down to the provost marshals every night and sleep there on the floor to be ready if wanted. The provost marshal's is over a mile from here. We have a good many men go every day to the city hall where the draft has been taken place and they are now examining the drafted men or their substitutes. Most of them get substitutes. Every night the men that the examining board are listed under a strong guard and taken to a barracks that is strongly guarded. A good many citizens are caught at the R.R. Depot trying to run away from the draft. Yesterday they arrested, while I was at the depot, a young fellow I should think about nineteen years old. He was dressed as a captain, only his coat was too large for him. He may have stolen or bought the coat. I have not heard how he came out.

I received a letter from Mary McNeill a few days since. Guess I will answer this letter soon. I waited so long before answering the other that I thought she would not answer it. Have not heard from Alex yet; wish he would write. Have you heard from him lately; if you have I will write to him again. I think James is not getting along so badly as you said in your last letter. I expect a letter from him soon. Did you receive that $20.00 check that I sent you two or three weeks since by mail? You said nothing about it in your last letter. As we can get plenty of reading here you need not send me the Observer; send only the Tribune once in a while.

They are now giving furloughs in this reg't. I think I told you that James Lucas was reduced to the ranks and loses a month's pay for being concerned in stealing rations. A corporal here has an easier time than a private, as he only changes the guard, and does not stand guard. Also he does not come on duty as often as a private. Capt. Burdick has resigned and is going home very soon, I think. Every day a small quantity of whiskey is given to each man that wants it. Some kind of medicine is in it; I think it is quinine. They only commenced giving it out a day or two ago. All in the Co. that want it are marched to the hospital to get it from an open window. Some would drink the whiskey, no matter what was in it, for the sake of the spirits. I write in haste so I must close.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

P.S. Please write soon.

author: charles
location: Camp Davis, Capitol Hill, Washington, D.C.
transcription:
Sept. 15, 1863
Camp Davis, Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I received the Tribune two or three days since, and yesterday rec'd. a letter from Alex. He was well and having a pleasant time.

I think you have the wrong idea about the no. of demerits that the cadets can get before they are found. I came across one of James' old letters and in it he said that they can had 150 demerits the first six months, also the same for the second six months of the first year. After that 100 demerits in six months will discharge them. It takes 150 demerits in six months to discharge them the first year. Have you heard from James lately? How is he getting along and how did he dispose of all his photographs? I think James will get along well enough, but don't expect he will graduate very high. Has Hiram I. got his appointment yet?

There is a good deal of sickness in this regiment. A corporal from our Co. died a few days since. He was apparently a stout, rugged fellow, about twenty-one years old, I should think. Alex Douglas is not very well he is this finest, but you will have a chance to see him for yourself, as he expects to go home soon on a furlough. Pet Steais is in the hospital which is close to the barracks. They live well in the hospital and he comes over to the barracks sometimes. Something is the matter with his chest, I believe.

The boys in our Co. laugh a great deal at one of our men, also pity him because he was such a fool as to do as he did. It seems he was engaged to a girl before he enlisted and he has sent her pay, bounty, and other money to the amount of $200. A few days since he heard that she was married and had spent all the money. He is an ignorant fellow and can neither read nor write. The men told him often that she would have served him so and that he had better send it to his father. When asked how his girl is, he replies that she has gone to Hell. This word is rather common here used in this way "keep on if you think there is no hell."

There is a good deal of talk about our leaving this place soon. I don't know whether we will or not. We are to receive our pay today. If we do leave here I shall be sorry, for it is a good place. A short time since we learned that we could draw books from the soldier's free library in the city. Since then we have drawn books.

author: charles
transcription:
Oct. 31, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd the letter and box brought by Alex, who arrived here the 29th. Am very much obliged for all the nice things you sent which were unaccounted. The dried apples though, I don't know exactly what to do with, as I will have to buy sugar for them. I will have plenty of socks for this winter as I now have five pairs.

Yesterday our Lieut. called me to him and asked me if I wanted a furlough. I told him I did not at present. A good many are going home on furlough now so as to vote at the N.Y. elections. But the most are sick furloughs. A good many will leave tonight for home. I have only about $1.50 in money which would be very little to go home with. I can get transportation and have it taken out of my next pay. Also I got transportation part of the way. Last night I saw Capt. Rich. He asked me if I had my word to send home as he was going to C. I told him I was better. For about a week I had a cough and very little appetite and for that time did not do my duty. For two or three days I took cough mixture. I have now been on duty several days and feel all right again.

Today we are to be mustered in for pay. I think I have told you a careless thing I did while we were at Alexandria. I would carry what money I had of in my vest pocket for safe keeping as I would sometimes lose my pocketbook out of my pants at night. Well, I carried a comb and looking glass in the same pocket and in pulling one of these out I suppose I jerked out a five dollar bill. I never found the $5.00 of course, as there are plenty of dishonest soldiers. Also D. said 50¢ charges on the box which is 28¢ apiece for us. I guess Alex's chance for getting into the Invalid Corps is small. I think Alex will not want to be transferred into it.

I will write to James in a few days and send him that letter. What do you think about his prospects? I think Frances will enjoy vacation when it comes, as she has to work so hard. This teaching school would try my temper, I think.

Yesterday I read a letter from Corbeau, in which a mother told her son that she had let out his sheep on double in four years, and is to receive a lb. of wool yr. head yearly besides. That is better than you did with your sheep. We have some fine singers in this reg't. Two or three nights I have heard some our reg't. serenading the Col. It sounded very nice. They sung, "Let me kiss him for his mother" and two or three more songs I do not know the names of. Steais is in the hospital again; complains of his breast.

Today there is a detail of Sergts. and Corporals to go off somewhere with three days rations. I wrote you sometime since that I went to Point Lookout near Fortress Monroe. Well, I happened to look on a map and found that Point Lookout is at the mouth of the Potomac and it near the south of Chesapeake Bay as I wrote you. It is a long ways from there to F. Monroe. I think a good many N.Y. soldiers will be home to vote at the election Tuesday. Moses Cokey will leave tonight for Champlain. I think. Please write as often as you can. I hope you will settle with the Savages immediately. Hoping that you will make yourself comfortable this winter, I will close.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: mother
transcription:
Nov. 15th, 1863
Champlain, N.Y.

My Darling Child:

Yours of the 1st of Nov. was rec'd. yesterday, and quite overwhelmed us with joy, for I had almost despaired of hearing from you again. We were beginning to have our forebodings. Sometimes we had you in Libby prison, sometimes all mangled in a field hospital, and at others, with our blessed lamented Henry among the "unknown" dead. You can imagine the set of your letters upon us. All our friends are rejoicing with us for they thought we had reason to be anxious. Mrs. Brinkerhoff came to me in church today and whispered "Have you heard from Alexander?" Her countenance beamed with joy when I answered in the affirmative. We know that Geary's Division was engaged in the last battle, although we are no member of the 60th, but we feared most that you were among the prisoners captured with the wagons. You must write us often for this anxiety of mind tells upon my poor shattered nervous system. I read a letter from James with yours. He will write you soon, so I will not transcribe his letter. He has had little leisure for writing, not as much as he had last year. I hope you will be here next summer to meet him. I can but hope that this terrible war is nearly over, that the rebellion is in its death throes. I rejoice that Charles was not in the last battle in Virginia. His reg't., fortunately was not among those sent out from Washington to the front at that time. I expect every mail to hear that they have been ordered away for I see it announced that the "Invalid Corps" only will be retained in Washington.

I am sadly disappointed in not obtaining your discharge. Your Col. wrote me that he "would do what he could to restore you to me, but feared the attempts would be futile." I am gratified at the good character he gives you and I hope you will continue to merit the approbation of your officers. I feel as your former Col. D. "that my claim upon you is stronger than country, even." I hope to have you yet. In the meantime take good care of yourself for my sake, as well as your own, physically, morally, and spiritually. Do not neglect the cultivation of your mind and morals. The habits you form in the army will attend you through life. I warn you against the "yellow covered" literature. I need not repeat to you what I have so often said about reading. Use no language that is in the slightest not pure. Never indulge in unworthy phrases. Be gentlemanly in your conversation and manners. Remember your promise to me. I think of it with pleasure. Never forget for one instant that you are a professed Christian. "Go and tell Jesus" all your trials. His ear is ever open, and more than that. His kind sympathizing heart is ready, to comfort, to heal. Go to Him for guidance, for wisdom, for submission, for every needed grace. Cast all your burdens upon him and He will sustain you, for he never fails. Keep near Him in prayer. Like the great and good Havelock, be a Christian soldier. Do nothing to bring reproach upon the blessed name of the Saviour. And may He keep you, my darling boy, in the hollow of His hand and restore you soon to me, is the daily prayer of your affectionate

Mother

I hope you will get a Thanksgiving dinner somewhere. I wish I could send you one. I trust you will be with us next year. I shall not go out this year. How can I when all my boys are away! I cannot.

author: alexander
transcription:
Dec. 1st, 1863
General Hospital
Tullahoma, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I presume you will be surprised to hear from me from this place. Well here I am in the hospital. I was wounded at the storming of Lookout Mountain. I am not seriously hurt. I am wounded in my left side by a minie ball. Rather a close call for my life, I think. I shall soon be back to the regiment. God has been very good to me. Company H lost as follows as near as I can learn: George Hays, killed; Sergeants Hubbell and Long, Corporals Ish and Kelly, Private Sidney Rider, wounded. I am not positive whether Sergt. Long was wounded or not. Latter was all right the last I saw or heard of him. We made a grand bayonet charge at Lookout. The rebs ran like good fellows. He took the whole posse (1800) prisoner. Please write often and direct as usual. I think I shall be with the regt. soon. Love to all.

Your affectionate son

Alexander F. Hubbell

author: mother
transcription:
Dec. 9th, 1863
Champlain, N.Y.

My Darling Child:

Where are you? Oh, where are you? Not a word have I heard from you since the late battles in Tennessee and I am in the deepest distress about you for I should have heard from you ere this, if all was well with you. I write without knowing where this letter may find you, whether with your Reg't., in hospital, or in prison. As yet your name is absent from the heart breaking list. I shrink from looking at the long dark catalogues. How many hearts have been made desolate in the taking of Lookout Mountain. I pray that the more dark wars may roll over me, for I am nearly engulfed in the billows. Oh, how they lash my poor tempest tossed, stricken heart. Dear, dear, precious Henry. I cannot dwell a moment upon his fate without an agony that is almost insupportable.

I cannot purchase the things you sent for till I know that you have come safely out of the battles. If you have been cast on Belle Island you would never receive them. God forbid that you should ever have a home there even for a day. Perhaps you have written and your letter got reached me. I know you would not keep me in an agony of suspense. If you were in hospital, some of your comrades surely would write me.

I rec'd. a letter from Chas. yesterday. He is still in Washington awaiting orders since they were relieved by the Invalid Corps. He is very anxious to hear from you since Hooker's battle. I have sent you stamps in almost every letter; have sent you envelopes as in newspapers and letters. If they are not rec'd, it is not worth while to send any more. Let me know if they are. I have selected material for your shirts which I like very much. The price will be a little over four dollars. I cannot get boots made for less than five dollars and a half. I can get them at the store for $3.75, said to be good. Socks for 60¢. Altogether, including the express charges it will amount to about fifteen dollars. I wish you would send without delay the measure of your foot or the number you wear.

Are you not glad you were not with Meade in his late retreat? The Army of the Potomac has a hard fate. Grant must come up and throw his wand over it and it will go.

James' examination is new. I hope he will be successful. Take good care of yourself. What a happy day it will be when you come home to stay. Then the silence of this great castle will be broken which is so painful now. Mrs. Ransom says Col Goddard's name is on the list of killed or wounded. I hope it is not serious. Write me immediately, my precious boy, and write as often. May God keep you "in the hollow of His hand," be a shield and buckler to you, preserve you from all evil and soon restore you to us is the daily prayer of your

Anxious and affectionate

Mother

author: alexander
transcription:
Dec. 13th, 1863
Wauhatchie, East Tennessee

Dear Charley:

I presume you have about come to the conclusion that I have left the land of the living or else entirely forgotten you, but it is no such thing. I have not forgotten you, though I would not blame you for thinking so. I know I have been sadly negligent, but still a great many things have conspired to prevent my writing — the want of materials for the main. I am now writing upon paper I received today. Now for business!

We had a great time coming out here. Were stationed for some time upon the Nashville and Chattanooga railroad, which the 1st Division of our Corps still guards. We (the 2nd Div.) went with Gen. Hooker to open the road to Chattanooga. Five regts. of the Division had a big fight with Longstreet, the night of the 28th of Oct, and thrashed him soundly. I — hours previous we were sent to hold a gap in the mountains on the border of Georgia at a place called Whiteside. So you see we just missed the fight. Three regts of our brigade were engaged. Gen'l Greene, commander of brigade, was wounded. Gen. himself slightly wounded in the toe.

The 60th has been in three fights since then. Our Division was the one chosen to storm Lookout Mountain. I hope you may never be called on to climb such a hill as that. We were often required to halt ourselves on with our hands, which you know, in the face of the enemy is not over pleasant. We sit and look at each other very composedly as we have both learned better manners than to fire at each other. The rebels are very anxious to exchange papers with us, but we have strict orders not to do it. If the settling of the war was left to the soldiers we would do it in short order. Some of the Rebs are pretty nice fellows, much to my surprise.

My wound caused me to miss the fights of Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. The loss of the Co. stands as follows: Lemage, Tees, Rider, Small, Hubbell, wounded; Majo, Doten, Housedean, killed. The last I saw or heard of him. We made a grand bayonet charge at Lookout. The rebs ran like good fellows. He took the whole posse (1800) prisoner.

I shall endeavor to be more punctual in writing hereafter. Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon and I am afraid I would not receive the letter.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Dec. 16th, 1863
Wauhatchie, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I am again with the regt. and doing duty. My side is still pretty sore but then I manage to get along first rate. My wound caused me to miss the fights of Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. I did not like the way things worked at the hospital and told the surgeon I was ready to go back to the regt. Two others of the regt. came back with me. We are back again in our old camp and we are pretty hard up for rations. The whole army is in the same way. We are on half rations. The railroad will be open in a few days and we shall have abundance soon.

Old Bragg is pretty well used up and will be wiped out before long, I think. The Regt. was in two battles since I left — Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. Loss of Company H. is as follows: Doten and Michael Housedean, killed; Alfred Lemage and Thomas Small, wounded. Thos. Small had his leg torn off.

I have only a small bit of candle left and must close. Give my regards to Capt. Ransom and let him know the loss of the Co. Love to all. Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon and I am afraid I would lose the letter.

Hoping to see you all soon, I remain

Your Aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Sergt. Long was not hurt.

author: charles
transcription:
Jan. 3, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I wish you and Frances a happy New Year. Did either of you pass a pleasant New Year's day? I was on guard but passed it well enough. On that day we had boiled flour pudding for supper. It was new business for our cooks and they put the puddings on the bottom of the kettles; one burst and burst the bag; the other two were then raised from the bottom of the kettles by a string tied to them and fastened to the floor above. The pudding was not very good; the raisins were the best part of it. On Christmas we had for dinner 8 turkeys — price $11.50; 2 kegs of lager beer, price $5.50; and a baked bread pudding with raisins in it. The dinner was bought with Co. Funds. I do not like beer so did not drink any. A good many of the boys got quite happy on it.

Christmas morning an Irishman belonging to our Co. was found at the side of the road dead drunk by one of our men. He shouldered him and brought him into camp as if he had been a dead pig. The Irishman says he was having his Christmas.

A good many of the old regts. are reenlisting for three years or the war. They get a 30 days furlough and a large bounty. Their reenlistment is dated from the time they get their furlough and not from next summer when their time is out. In this way the soldier gains several months time. I think Alex had better not reenlist although he can get $1,000 bounty.

Two or three nights since our regt. and the 14th New Hampshire received marching orders with three days rations, but the order was countermanded next day. We were to go to "Hardsburger" or Harper's Ferry and some back in a few days, but they say that if we had once left here we would not have come back. A Brigade from Meade's Army went, so we did not have to go. When we hear about marching orders we don't believe it because it is an old story. We still believe we are going when the knapsacks are on our backs.

Our regt. has done a good deal in the stealing line lately taking turkeys, chickens, etc. A woman came running into our guard house for a guard, saying a soldier stole a turkey and a piece of meat right before her face. Of course she did not get a guard, for the soldier was not going to stay there and be arrested. A guard could not have found him. Most of our regt. are good men but there are some great rascals in it.

Who surveyed the wood land and how much did it cost? I think from what you wrote the surveyors found the true line. Enclosed I send you a letter from Alex that I received about a week since. I forgot to tell you in my other letters that I saw Geo. Dodds some time ago. He came from the hospital to see us Champlainers. He had been sick with a fever and was not then entirely well. Please write soon.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Feb. 18, 1864
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you a day or two at on from Louisville, Ky., but you recollect I promised to write you as often as possible — and as I have plenty of leisure at present, I don't know as I can better occupy it than by writing you. You agree with me perfectly, I know.

We left Louisville early yesterday morning and reached here a little before dark last night. Strange to say, we had comfortable passenger cars instead of the cold freight cars we expected. To leave here at three this afternoon. I was out in the city this morning on a pass. I went to hospital No. 8 and saw one of our wounded boys, Thos. Small, who lost his leg at Ringgold. He was doing well and seemed very cheerful.

Luther has spent the greater part of his state bounty — and I don't see as he is any the better for it. Mr. Marshall Dunn said the state bounty yet "please give him five dollars as a reward for his services." He allows the boys to give him what they will. All who have received the bounty have given him five dollars and I would not be "behind hand."

How does Frances and her school flourish? Mrs. Rider and Miss Riley? Have Frances, Miss Averill, and others been down in the ravine to have a slide yet? Tell Frances I shall endeavor to write her soon. All the boys from Champlain are well. Direct your letters in future to Nashville, Tenn., Army of the Cumberland. They will reach me if you direct to Washington, but will come sooner, I think, by directing the other way, to Nashville. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Feb. 21, 1864
Stephenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

It is a most beautiful Sabbath morning. The sun is shining warm and pleasant, the birds are singing, and every thing is hushed to an unusual quiet. It is such a day as is seldom vouchsafed to us soldiers. Nevertheless all are on the alert. The horse thief Morgan is on the move with a force of some eight thousand men and there is no telling upon what particular part he will fall. All the troops stationed here, with the exception of our regt., were under arms last night. All his motions are watched and I am afraid he will find it hard to come upon our troops unprepared.

We reached here night before last and — most wonderful to relate — found a Soldier's Home established here where we were provided with an excellent supper and good sleeping accommodations. Yesterday we established our camp and commenced carrying timber to build our shanties. Today most of us are resting from our labors. My three tent mates and myself had a confab together and came to the conclusion that we would not work upon our shanty today as soldiers above all needed God's blessing — and Sabbath breaking would not be very likely to get it. My tent mates are Corporal Kelly, Oliver Lafountain, and George Bully. Two of them you have seen.

Opposite our camp a large number of soldiers are buried — victims of Chickamauga. After that battle the General Hospital was established here and these men died from the effects of their wounds.

The veterans of 64 attached to the 60th N.Y. had a warm welcome from the old 3rd Brigade when they reached here. (A gentleman attached to the Christian Com., I cannot, just gave me a paper entitled "the Parlor Visitor." So you see I have something good to read today.) The Brigade Band gave them a grand serenade accompanied by lusty cheers from the men of the Brigade present which were promptly responded to by the Veterans. "The Old Sixtieth" is of some account down here, you see.

I have talked with a number of rebs since I came here. They all tell the same story of want and discouragement in the rebel ranks. I was talking with a rebel Capt. of Cavalry yesterday. "Yes," said he in conclusion to what he was saying in regard to the rebel conscription, "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts." One of the rebs told me that it was generally believed in the rebel army that this war will terminate about June. He says Johnson's (formerly Bragg's) army swear that they will not stand in the next battle.

Gen'l. Slocum made a speech here not long since in which he prophesied a speedy termination of the war. There does not seem to be any doubt of the war's terminating this year.

I have done my best to go into minute details. I am afraid you will get sick of it. If you do let me know. Tell Frances I shall certainly write her soon if it be possible. Love to all.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

Gave you heard from James yet? Be particular when you direct your letters to put on the Brigade, Division of Corps, also Army of the Cumberland. The bugles are blowing the dinner call. I must hurry up. One of the rebs said, "You think you took a great many prisoners at the last fight, and so you did, but wait until the next fight and you will be prisoners."

author: charles
transcription:
April 25, 1864
Hd. Qtrs. Dept of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Alex:

I rec'd your letter of Apr. 10th yesterday and was very glad to hear from you. Have been waiting to hear from you before I wrote, so that I could have your direction. It is a very long direction. Would you not get your letters as quickly if it was shortened?

I am relieved from duty at these Hd. Qtrs, and ordered to rejoin my regt., but have been waiting the last two or three days for the boat. Will probably go off tomorrow. I am to carry the mail on my way back to Gen. Banks Hd. Qtrs. in the field, as by so doing I will receive subsistence on the boat and a state room. This is better than carrying my rations with me and sleeping anywhere. I will have a long ride up the R. River, which is better than footing it as the army have done. Do you see my being here has done me so much good. There has been a great fight near R. River in which we lost a great many men and I am not sorry I was not in that fight. Another battle is expected soon. The army is amassed on R. River at Grand Encore so then I will ride all the way. My penmanship is not good enough is the reason of my going back to the regt. But I feel well enough about going back as others have failed to suit as well as me. Just before I came two men were relieved and now another new clerk that has come, I think, will be relieved as he does not write very well and he has not been set to work.

A clerk here was killed a short time since. He came in drunk one night about 12 o'clock and after spreading his mattress on the floor of the office where he slept, went out on the gallery on the third story, and as he was about todescend a few steps that led to a lower part of the gallery he pitched headlong over the bannister and struck the stone pavement on his head in the yard below. He never moved. A lot of us soon gathered around to see him. He was in his drawers and shirt as he was just going to bed. All the clerks attended at his burial. He was buried by the hospitals. A wagon from the hospital containing eight bodies followed by another wagon containing a corporal and eight men drove into the cemetery. As the chaplain could not be there that day one of the clerks made a prayer, the volleys were soon fired, and we got into the street car and came home.

I am sorry that James does not let us know where he is. Hope he will come out all right. How do you prosper? Are you in good health? Hope you will try and take good care of yourself. Give my regards to Luther. Have you got your watch yet and does it keep good time? I have rec'd but two letters, yours and Mothers, since I left Washington. Expect to find several with the regt.

The street cars here are drawn by one mule and some of them have two stories, that is, people ride on top of the cars and in it. The honesty of the passengers is trusted to put the fare in the box, as there is no conductor.

The Army on the R. River under Gen. Banks expects to soon drive the rebs out of Louisiana and I think will do it. I will be there to help, if not sick. Did you ever hear anything about the dry Tortugas? It is a small island on the coast of Florida where Uncle Sam is building an immense fort. A great many soldiers are sentenced to hard labor on this island for various crimes. A good many are sent from this city, for five or ten years.

I hope you will prove a better correspondent than you have been so far. Do try and write often and I will answer them. Will close by wishing you good luck.

From your aff. brother,

C. F. Hubbell

author: james
transcription:
Aug. 15th, 1864
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Mother and Fannie:

It is a long while since I have written you. I think my last letter was from Morganza. Since that time our regt. has seen considerable hardship. We left Louisiana the last of June for the North — this, I think Charlie has written you. As soon as we arrived at Washington D.C. we were sent out to the defenses and placed in the rifle pits. The next morning there was heavy skirmishing near us, but the Rebs retreated and we saw nothing of them. The next day we were sent as a reserve for the 6th Corps and followed the Rebs out to the Shenandoah Valley, the 6th Corps following close and skirmishing, but the Johnnies did not want to fight. We crossed a day and the next we crossed the river and lay in a belt of woods all day expecting a fight, but no, the enemy only wanted to get off with their plunder and keep us off, and they did it. At night we received orders to report at Washington within 24 hours. "Fall in!" ran along the lines and off we marched, many with light eyes and gloomy feelings — the prospect of marching all night does not lighten the feelings of many. Just as we were starting four men came in with a large dressed porker but it was goodly big, for a soldier cannot carry more than his usual load. Pig hitting had gone on pretty briskly that afternoon. Some were fortunate enough to get their pork for supper. Hardtack and coffee was all most of us had to eat. Do you know what hardtack is! Bake a flour and water cake with no salt or saleratus on a griddle till it is hard — throw it on a shelf for three or four days and see what kind of a meal it will make.

We waded the river and with an occasional half hour rest marched until four the next day. I stood it until about eight the next morning and then the want of sleep and food, a blistered foot and fatigue compelled me to fall out. The wagon train soon came along. I put my gun and bundles on one and found I could get along. I kept with this train until we arrived at Chainbridge within the defenses of W. There we consumed. Orders were soon issued to prepare for field service; shoes and clothes were given out, and after a day's rest off we started. Where we went I did not know or care. After several days hard marching the two corps pitched camp about two miles beyond Harper's Ferry. Then came a counter march. Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination, the men in the meantime becoming worn out. At Frederick City I was taken to a hospital where I am now and have been two weeks. I was quite sick but am now pretty well and expect soon to go to a convalescent camp. My sickness was generally unwell and played out. The hospital is pleasantly situated on a hill overlooking the city. Papers are brought in every morning with war and city news. They do not apprehend a draft here — the wards are fast filling out their quotas. Milk is retailed at 16 cents a quart; peaches are selling at 80 cents a bushel. I had a little change and could buy fruit. We get tea four a cent here.

There is a general feeling indignation expressed in these papers that our Generals should not have ascertained the actual force of the enemy and prevented them from coming so near our Capitol. They state that we had twenty thousand troops around Washington, part of them veterans, while the actual forces of the Rebels was 15,000, since ascertained. The fact that the army came up here with that force, harvested, plundered and got off with a wagon train three miles in length is rather irritating to us.

About Charlie's health — he was quite thin and used up when I left; he finds the marches very hard. Charlie is one of the kind that'll go until he cannot go. I do not think that is the way. He remarked that if he was sick he would not have vital energy enough to recover. A good rest and something to eat would set him all right, I think. I hope he has been sent off. Charlie is pretty plucky and won't give up, but I think he ought to favor himself more.

This paper was given me when we arrived at Washington from Louisiana. This I have carried since then which accounts for its being soiled. Our fare here is soft bread or pilot bread, meat twice a day, stewed apples at night.

It seems to me that I should like to come up with the Johnnies and have a good hard fight with them instead of dogging them day and night and then having them get away marching and countermarching, accomplishing nothing, I do not like. What is the news in C? Will they be obliged to draft them in Sept.? Please write soon. Direct as before.

James

author: alexander
location: 2d Div. Hospital, 20th Corps, near Atlanta, Ga.
transcription:
Aug. 22, 1864
2d Div. Hospital — 20th Corps
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

You perceive that I am again in the hospital. I am not wounded but am afflicted with what the surgeon calls genuine scurvy. He says I am very young to have it. By taking good care of myself and with proper nourishment (vegetables) I think I shall soon be fit for duty.

I received your letter of August 8th yesterday. Dixon brought it down to me. You may be sure I was pleased for I had not heard from you since the 25th of July. I have received several papers since then. You did not send me a Tribune with an acct. of the battle of the 20th. I should like to see it. If you can, please send it or any other paper with an acct. of it.

Nothing of special interest has transpired since I last wrote — yes, there has too, if the report is true. Very heavy artillery and musketry firing was heard a day or two since to the right of the line and the report of the affair is that a heavy battle came off there, the rebels charging and recharging our works, but were repulsed each time with terrible slaughter. Their loss, it is said, is to be counted by the thousand. The rebels are reported to have been very much under the influence of liquor. Reports are so conflicting that I hardly dare write them. Of a battle having taken place I have but little doubt as the firing was very sharp. You must bear in mind that our line is many miles long and we can only judge what is going on by the firing. There are so many rumors afloat that you can hardly tell what is reliable till you see the papers.

Please send papers often and a magazine now and then if convenient. Please write soon and often. Lieut. Brookway has taken charge of my mail and will forward it to me wherever I am. Please send me some stamps. I will use my last when I send this. I found the two stamps I lost. Mrs Frances yet returned? Tell her I received her letter and didn't see my boots for a week after. I will endeavor to write to her soon. I wrote James and Charles a few days since. I hope that they will write me. I think your fears are groundless about their being prisoners. Love to all. F. A. Cook is at Champlain, and he is hot for Lincoln. I will hoist my colors soon. If I live I shall cast a vote this fall. You know I will have been in the service over three years when the election comes off, and according to the laws of the U.S. I shall be of proper age to vote, as no one is received into the U.S. Service under 18. By the muster rolls I shall be over 21.

Your aff. Son

Alex F. Hubbell

author: charles
transcription:
Aug. 26, 1864
Camp near Harper's Ferry

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you last night dated Aug. 20th, was glad to hear from you, but am very sorry you are so anxious about James and me. James, I think, is all right. When around for a couple of days near Frederick James was sent to the hospital at that place, and Dr. Sweeney told me that he would send me as soon as he could but would not at that time very well. James was thin in flesh and had the diarrhea. If he has been very sick since then the doctors have made him so with their medicine. But I think James is having a good time in some hospital or convalescent camp — that is, a good time compared with marching. I have not heard from James nor have I written him. It is useless to be anxious about him because he has not written. You know, he doesn't seem to care about letter writing. Perhaps he is waiting till he rejoins the regt. As for myself I am well and have been nearly two weeks in the convalescent dept. As there are more clerks here than are necessary I may go back to the regt. any day, and then I may not. There is a good deal of work to do but then we live well. I have flatted in considerably since I have been here because I eat all the sugar I want, for one thing. You have been sending me recipes for the diarrhea, because I suppose as it is an army complaint you think I must have it. I have been troubled very little with it. I know a man with whom it has become chronic, who is a perfect skeleton. He has a good appetite and does duty all the time.

I am sorry you wasted $5 telegraphing about James. Dr. Sweeney told me at the time James was sent to the hospital that he would be sent on to Washington probably, and as I did not know his address I have not written him. James had no chevrons on his coat and I guess in his paper for admission to the Hospital Corporal was not written. I hope you will not worry about us boys, for if there is anything the matter with us you will hear of it. You must call no news good news. I am entirely out of money and postage stamps. When you would send me a couple of dollars and some stamps. You direct the letters me right. I have recd 2 or 3 letters lately from you, also two newspapers. Have not written because I have not had the material or time. We have been on the move nearly all the time, have been here two days. Our Army is composed of the 19th and the 6th Corps — also the 8th — all under the command of General Sheridan who has a large force of cavalry with him. We have not had a sight of the rebs yet, although the cavalry has fought with them some; also a few of the infantry. Please write often. It is not convenient for me to write as I have no place to carry writing materials and not much time, but I will write as often as I can. Give my love to Frances. Also don't forget yourself.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Aug. 30/64
2d Div. Hospital, 20th A.C.

Dear Mother:

Now that I am in a hospital I know you will be anxious to hear from me often and consequently I shall endeavor to be very regular in my correspondence. I am getting along as well as can be expected, though I expect will take some little time to get this scurvy out of my blood. I have very good care taken of me so you need not be troubled on that score.

I received your letter of Aug 16th day before yesterday and am glad to hear that you at home are well, and very, very sorry to hear that James is sick in hospital and Charley likely to be soon. Please excuse me, Mother, but I did have a hearty laugh when I took in the idea of your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time. I suppose you think it is something that should not be laughed at. Well I agree with you on that point — it is not quite so funny as it might be. Low diet and doctor's medicines are not quite as agreeable as some things.

A truce to the blues and now for something lively. Our Corps has fallen back from Atlanta and is now holding a line along the Chattahoochee. The rest of the army I expect has gone on a grand flanking excursion, heading toward Macon. It is reported here today that the rebs have left Atlanta and gone after Sherman. I expect stirring things will happen in a day or two. General Slocum now commands our 6th Corps. 1st Lieut. P. H. Brookway (formerly Orderly Sergt. of Co. H.) now commands our Co. Capt. Delaney, as you are aware, is at home. There is very little of interest to write. I hope the chronic diarrhea will not get hold of James and Charles. It is a terrible disease. Love to all. Please send some stamps.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
Sept. 2d, 1864
U. S. General Hospital
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

The evening of the day I wrote you my last letter, I with a large number of other sick and wounded was put on board a hospital train and sent to this place. We were two nights and a day getting here. We should have gone directly to Nashville, but old Wheeler had made a raid and torn up the road so we were obliged to stop here. I do not know how long we shall remain here. Generally as soon as the men are able to hear it they send them on to Nashville. I was pretty sick yesterday and last night, but am very much better today. I shall be able to join the regt. before a great while, I think. Considerable anxiety is felt to know who the Presidential nominee is at the Chicago convention the 29th inst. We will know in a day or two. There is nothing of interest to write. Send your letters to the regt. as usual. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

author: alexander
location: U.S. Field Hospital No. 2, Chattanooga, Tennessee
transcription:
Sept. 18, 1864
U. S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Much to my gratification a day or two since the 60th N.Y. Vets. were sent to this place from the front to escort the Paymaster of the 20th Corps down, and of course they brought what mail there was for me at the Regt. (5 letters.) You can rest assured I was well pleased for I had not heard from you in a long, long, time, and I did not dare have the mail sent here for I was liable to be sent off to Nashville or some other place any time. Direct your letters to the regt. as usual. There is too much uncertainty to have them directed here. I am getting along pretty well, but how soon I shall be fit for duty I am unable to say. I may be well soon and it may take a long time to get this misnamed scurvy out of my blood. However I guess I will be all right before long. The man that gives out the medicine has just been around and given me a gay old drink of lime water — something very similar to lemonade. Then I say lime I don't mean lime such as they make mortar of, but limes, a fruit like lemons.

Luther is with the regt. He has been up to see me twice. A number of the boys have been up to see me. It is pleasant to have them here. The regt. is still here unless they have left this morning. I am sorry I shall not be able to draw pay with the regt. this time. Government owes me some two hundred and forty dollars. I may draw a little pay here, sufficient for my wants but no more.

What do the people of C. think of the draft. We all like it down here. There is no way to put down this rebellion but by force of arms. A few more vigorous pushes will shove them into the Atlantic Ocean.

When you speak in your letters of the tomatoes you are having, and the new potatoes, etc., etc. in such abundance, I long to be there to enjoy these good things with you, and I hope I shall before many months roll around. The letters I received from you were of Aug. 24th and 29th. The other letter was from Jack Ingram. I received six stamps in one of your letters which will do for some little time. I received the money and everything you sent except the tea, I think. Perhaps you did not put on enough postage for the tea. Tell Fannie I will try and write her before a great while. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. B. If any body wants to know my political principles you tell them I am a "war man." That's enough. Please write often.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

I am glad to see the copper heads don't like McClellan. It speaks well for him.

author: charles
location: In the field near Strasburg, Virginia
transcription:
Sept. 21st, 1864
In the field near Strasburg

Dear Mother:

I sit down to write you a few lines, feeling very thankful that James came out of the battle near Winchester two days since unhurt. There were four killed and twelve wounded in our Co. James is looking very well, he got nicely recruited at the hospital. A day or two after Dr. Sweeney wrote James rejoined the regt. Dr. Sweeney is very kind to James and me, and some time since wished me to transfer him to you. I am still with the Brigade Commissary and am getting fat, the result of good living. I have to walk on the march but carry no load.

I rec'd your letter with the $2.00 and stamps, also James rec'd three newspapers with Mr. Hoyle's name on them. James got our Capt. to write to Albany for his state bounty which is twenty-five dollars and ordered it sent to you. He should have had it long since. The letter was sent a few days since. I think the money you invested in the "2d hands" may well pay. It may be well to invest some of our money in the capital of the C. Bank, but will leave you to do as you think best.

We were camped near Berryville two weeks and while there our Regt. drilled twice a day, leaving hardly time to cook. That is the reason James has not written. We lost a good many men in the fight two days since, but whipped the rebs and drove them to this place where they are making a stand, but they will soon have to leave. Our regt. lost 55 wounded and 10 killed. We are now about twelve miles this side of Winchester. Am glad to hear that you and Frances are well. We are pleased to hear from you so often, hope that you will continue to write often.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

(Written on back of this letter — a note from Frances.)

author: alexander
transcription:
September 21, 1864
U. S. Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Have you taken a realizing sense that I have now been in the U. S. Service as a soldier three years — three long — long — weary years! Yes — three years ago today I took an oath to serve the United States of America faithfully as a soldier for the term of "three years or the war," and I can conscientiously say that I have with God's help done my best to bear that oath and do my duty as a soldier should do. And now, dear Mother, I want you to join me, (and I know you will) in thanking God for his kind and watchful care over me in preserving me through so many dangers and temptations to which I have been exposed in the past terrible three years of war, and to ask a continuance of his kind care over me during the remainder of my term of service.

When I think of all the things which I have passed my heart is too full to speak. This is the first time since I have been in the service that I have been in a general hospital sick. You know I was in one last fall but then I was wounded and was only a short time from the regt.

Well, I wrote you, only a day or two since, and have nothing of special interest to communicate. I am getting along very well, I think. There is one very singular thing about it — as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat. However it may wear off in time. There are a number here troubled in the same way. Direct your letters to the regt. Give my regards to Mrs. B. Love to all,

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P.S. The morning papers give an acct. of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley. I am very anxious to hear from the boys.

author: alexander
location: U.S. Field Hospital No. 2, Chattanooga, Tennessee
transcription:
Sept. 21, 1864
U.S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Fannie:

I shall now only write an apology for a letter and shall conclude with a promise of a long letter before a great while, and I hope I shall find grace in your eyes. I do not feel very well today, and I trust you will regard this as a sufficient excuse for these few lines. I only write them to let you know I have not forgotten you. Please write me often.

Your aff. Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: alexander
location: U.S. Field Hospital No. 2, Chattanooga, Tennessee
transcription:
Sept. 25, 1864
U.S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Fannie:

Now for the long promised letter. You perceive I am still in the same place, but I am unable to say how long I may remain here. I am getting along very well, I think, and will doubtless be able to join the regt. before a very great while. I still continue to be blind at night. The Dr. thinks it will wear off in time. Others tell me I will never get over it, but then I think I shall.

How runs the political excitement in C? Pretty high I expect. It will be a very closely contested election, I think. A good many soldiers will vote for McClellan. A majority of the border state men, I think, will, and a large number of the "Hibernians." They don't like the "nigger" nor any man that favors them. The border men get quite wrathy over the idea of "nigger equality." They say they would rejoice to see the niggers free if they would be sent out of the country, lest to have the nection among them on an equality with the white man they never would agree to it. They say if they would be sent out of the country, they say they have talked with men from all the Northern states and none are willing to have them settle among them. They say the Northern states and none are willing to have them settle there, and are even more hostile to it than they are. "And now," said one, "what are you going to have packed on us what none of you are willing to receive! Never!!!"

I must confess, dear Fannie, that I sympathize strongly with these "border men" in this matter of what they call "nigger equality." I could never consent to see these black men mingled with our white and form a part of the people of the United States. I do not think it was ever the design of Providence that the two races should be mingled and I doubt not the Government will make some wise provision in this case. We have got enough on hand now to put down this rebellion. It will do to talk about this "equality" matter when the war is over.

Have you taken a realizing sense that I am now according to the laws of the United States twenty-one years of age and am privileged to vote at the coming elections. You know I have now been in the U. S. service a little over three years.

Sept. 27 — This morning the weather is quite chilly and threatens rain. It is very much like Sept. weather at home and makes me think of ripe apples and a thousand other good things. I should like tremendously to get hold of one of Mother's steamed apple dumplings. Perhaps before another year rolls round I shall be there to enjoy these good things.

The last letter I received from home was dated in August and I am very anxious to hear from you all, but I dare not have my mail sent here. I may be with the regt. soon. If not I believe I shall risk having it sent here. Continue to direct as before. Give my regards to Mrs. B. and all friends. Give much love to Mother.

Your aff. Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: james
transcription:
October 4, 1864
Harrisonburg
In the Shenandoah Valley

Dear Alex:

When did I write you last! I know it is a long time since. Do not think because I have not written you that I have forgotten you. We have had two fights of which you have undoubtedly heard, driving the rebels both times. The last pursuit the inhabitants of the towns through which we passed said the Rebs went through there with a rush, and that their army was demoralized. In the road in the pursuit during the night we passed several of their wagons burning. I do not believe that the Johnnies will make another stand here in the valley. You have travelled this road once, I think.

October 12th — Since I commenced this we have fallen back to Cedar Creek near Strasburg — burning barns and forage as we went. Alex Douglas has been boggled by the guerrillas, it is thought. He fell to the rear several days since with one man of our company while on a march and has not been seen or heard of since. The boys in this army have a habit of running through the houses and taking whatever they choose, which I think exasperates the rebels very much, and I cannot but fear for a straggler. This other fellow from our company was one of the greatest house thieves in our regt. Douglas was not any of that. I have heard this thief tell some of his stories. While he was in one house one of the children said, "Ma, there is a Yankee down cellar taking all our preserves and bacon." "Ma, see that Yankee looking in the oven." If they remonstrated with him he would "blackguard" them. I do not pity this fellow much. This running through houses is checked carefully by the officers but cannot always be prevented. Sometime before the battle of Winchester there was a little boy of our brigade gobbled while foraging. He was shot up with rebel deserters. During the fight they were ordered to turn out and help fight; he slipped out with them and made his escape. He said they were going to hang him for a spy.

Last night I received a letter from home. They want to know why we do not write. I have been rather negligent in writing. Charley has written several times but they have not received his letters; the mails have been irregular. Mother says you are quite ill. I hope you are better ere this. I have seen one month in the hospital since I enlisted. I'm all right now. Charley's health is now pretty good. There is some talk about our going to Louisiana. I hope we will not. I do not like the climate.

What are your views on the coming elections? I'm a voter; I go for old Abe; he is the man, I think. Little Mac will probably run strong. This war has lasted nearly four years. I would like to see it ended, and believe it will be soon.

Your aff. brother

James

author: charles
transcription:
Oct. 4, 1864
Harrisonburg

As the mail leaves soon I will write a few lines. I rejoined the regt. the last day of Sept. There were too many clerks there in the commissary so they told two of us to go to our regts. I am quite fat and am in good health. James is very well. I have no gun yet, as I turned in my gun when I left the regt. Expect to have one soon.

A few days since a recruit from Fresseville came to our Co. He rec'd. $1202 bounty. Enlisted for one year. We have been here three days. I don't know which way we will move from here. Have chased the rebs a long way. It is about ninety miles from here to Harper's Ferry. The cavalry have been as far as Stanton and have burned barns and grist mills. We advanced to the next town about 8 miles from here where we got a lot of flour and came back here the next day. The troops have suffered some from want of rations. Rations are wagoned here from Harper's Ferry. On the march the troops we foraged a great deal. Pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc. There is a Provost Marshall to stop such doings but it is done for all that. This is a rich valley — a fine farming country. There are a great many wounded rebs in the hospital here. We have also passed other towns where the rebs were in hospitals. They were sent this way after the fight near Bunker Hill.

Recruits are coming to this army fast. Quite a number have joined our regt. We have burned all the fences for a long ways around this place except where there is a safe guard. These oak rails make a good fire. This is a bad place to camp as water and wood are scarce. Have to go quite a distance for them. Do you know a soldier's daily duty? It is to cook, clean his gun and look over his clothes and pick off the vermin. On a march the soldiers get pretty lousy as they have no kettles to heat water to boil their clothes. It is a common saying that a man is no soldier unless he is lousy. Some of the men think that we are going to Louisiana to spend the winter. I hope not.

Have you rec'd seventy-five dollars from Albany — James' state bounty? James rec'd two or three days since two democratic newspapers (Journal of Commerce). We expect to receive a letter from you next mail. It is some time since we received one.

Charles

author: alexander
transcription:
Oct. 10th, 1864
U.S.A. Hospital No. 3
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You perceive I have again changed my quarters. I was sent from Chattanooga last Wednesday and reached here Friday morning. The hospital I am now in is a very good one and I am getting along famously. I asked the doctor this morning to let me go to my regiment. He said he would see about it. I think I shall go in a day or two. My eyes are much better.

The political excitement is running high. Lincoln seems to be the favored one. When we were coming from Chattanooga a vote was taken in the car I was in. Thirty-seven voted for Lincoln and five for McClellan. I tried to get a furlough while at Chattanooga but did not succeed. The doctor did not do right, I think. He gave a furlough to a fellow that had the scurvy not near so bad as I did, and when I asked him he said "he would like to but, but, but, etc."

I hope this war will be over before long and then I shall need no furlough. I am anxious to get back to the regt. so I can get hold of the lots of letters there are there for me. I expect there must be a lot. James and Charles have written me. There is little of interest to write. There is to be a flag raised and a political speech to be made at Fort Gillam today. If possible I shall go. Please write often. Love to all. Give my regards to Mrs. B.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: charles
transcription:
Oct. 22, 1864
Camp near Strasburg, Va.

Dear Mother:

James and I rec'd a lot of newspapers Oct. 18th and were anticipating a good deal of pleasure next day in reading them. Well, next morning I was awakened by a sharp volley of musketry. James exclaimed, "The Rebs are here!" We jumped up and put on our accoutrements and fell in behind our breastworks, but in a few minutes were ordered to pack up. We took our tents down in a jiffy. By that time the rebs were close to us. It was a surprise attack. They got behind our breastworks before we knew it. Our Brigade was ordered to leave our breastworks and form on the other side of a deep ravine. We jumped over the breastworks very quick as the Rebs were firing into us and we were moving up the hill the bullets came very thick. A good many of our men were shot here. James was wounded near this place. A Sergeant of our Co. says that as he was going to the rear with a wounded man he saw James; that James rec'd. a flesh wound in the thigh or hip and walked about five miles to the hospital. Says James had made a bandage of his drawers. He went with James to the hospital and says James is all right. James Lucas was reported killed, but I have since learned that he was taken to the hospital shot through the head and arm. Sergeant Pelkier (pronounced Pelky) from Corbeau of our town was shot through the leg. Alex Douglas has been missing about ten or twelve days. While on the march here, he and another man of our Co. were either captured or killed. It is supposed that they got to the rear and were taken prisoners by guerillas. Every one is very sorry about Douglas as he was very much liked. He and the other man were mounted. James Lucas wrote Mr. Douglas about Alex. Lieut. Col. Strain was wounded in the arm in the fight on the 19th of Oct. Our Regt. had about 50 wounded and 8 killed. Our Co. had 7 wounded and 2 killed.

The Rebs drove us out of our camp in the morning when we lost a great many men, but we rallied and drove them, recapturing all our artillery and all of theirs. We drove them out of our camp and beyond to Fisher's Hill. The Rebs came into our camp by the flank where the 8th Corps lay. I am very thankful that I did not get scratched. I think that I have received all your letters but am sorry that you have not received mine. I wrote two from Harrisburg. Am very sorry about Lucas. He rec'd a letter from home the night before the fight and intended to write the next day. Did you receive a letter from Dr. Sweeney some time since? He inquired of me if you did. Please write soon and send me a few stamps.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
transcription:
October 26th, 1864
U.S.A. Hospital No. 3
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You can have no idea how anxious I am to hear from you all and I have at length determined to have a letter directed here. So please, immediately on receipt of this, write me a long letter telling me all the news since last August — the date of the last letter I received from you, and do not fail to send it by return mail. I think I shall be here ten (and perhaps more) days longer.

I would not take the oath prescribed in the New York voting law and have consequently lost my chance of voting. Could I have voted I should have cast it "square and fair" for Abraham Lincoln. The majority of soldiers will vote that way.

Direct your letter simply to Nashville, Tenn. In case I am not here when it arrives I can write to Postmaster and have it sent on.

Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: james
transcription:
October 29th, 1864
Patterson Park Hospital
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Alex:

I had a letter written and sealed which I carried in my pocket for a long time. I have now determined to add another before I send it to you. I was wounded in the left thigh at Cedar Run. It is nothing but a flesh wound and is doing well. I walked several miles after being hit in order not to fall into the Johnnies hands. They were then driving our forces, but things changed before night. Our forces were driving them full well. Their army was completely demoralized. They threw away everything. We got their wagon train, artillery and almost everything they had. The Johnnies attacked and routed the eighth Corps before daylight. This rather took our force by surprise and compelled them to retreat as they were flanked and the breastworks would be of no use. I do not believe the Rebs will try it again in the Valley — three times terribly whipped.

Our Co. was very much cut up. It was also badly cut up at Winchester, so that there is scarcely anything left of it. Lucas was badly wounded. He is the only one you know in the company. Three fellows assisted me to the hospital which was situated in a barn several miles back. I had gone part of the way myself, but was about played out when they came along. I remained at the Hospital a day and was then sent on here. I had thirty miles to ride in an army wagon to get to a railroad station, and then one hundred and twenty in a freight car. That journey was a hard one.

The hospital here is a very comfortable one and the fare very good. Baltimore seems to be the first great place to which our wounded and sick are sent. They are transferred from here to Philadelphia. You were right when I heard from you last. I hope you have got well ere this. I look for a speedy termination of the war. I think we shall be able to judge a good deal come morning it is after the Presidential election. I shall be able to vote here and shall cast my vote for Abraham Lincoln. I hope he will be elected.

We have not been paid for six months. I think it is about time for the Paymaster to visit us. I do not know how long I will be here but will send you my address; it is Patterson Park Hospital, Baltimore, M.D.

Your affectionate Brother,

James.

author: charles
transcription:
Nov. 4, 1864
Camp at Cedar Creek, Va.

Dear Mother:

I read your letter announcing grandmothers death two days since. Was not surprised as she was so old. I suppose Aunt Mary will come North if she can get away.

Have not heard from James nor any of our wounded in the last fight. Two of our Co. who saw him say that his wound is not dangerous. Our Chaplain saw him in the hospital sitting up in bed. He told me James was doing well. I asked the Chaplain if his wound was serious. He said he did not know. I told him that James walked to the hospital. He then said it must be a flesh wound. Our Chaplain is none home sick. The badly wounded were at the hospital at Winchester. The others are forwarded on to the other hospitals. James Lucas, I heard, lay on the ground all day till he was taken up by an ambulance. I did not see him. However that I ought to write his folks, but if you will tell them that he was shot then he head and an arm it will do as well. Our Chaplain told me that he probably would not recover. I do not whether James is at Winchester or been sent on to some other city. The morning of the fight there were no ambulances and if a man could not walk he had to lay on the ground unless some of the soldiers carried him. Segt. Pelkier, of our town, shot in the leg, was carried by some of our Co. & left in a barn to be made prisoner of by the rebs as was supposed, but when we came back that night he was there.

We now drill & have dress parade, regular camp life. Do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. I do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. Did not know what had become of James until that night after dark.

Sunday, 6th: This morning we were called up at 4 oclock & fell into line with our arms. It looked as if they expected an attack, but after standing till daylight we broke ranks & cooked our breakfast. After eating we had Brigade Review & inspection.

I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co.

(Remainder of letter missing) From,

C. F. Hubbell (Charles)
